intro: Alabama is one of the few states that actually wrote a lost property law into its civil code. Title 35, Chapter 12 of the Code of Alabama spells out what a finder must do with something lost, and Alabama Code Section 35-12-3 even sets out that a finder is entitled to compensation for expenses reasonably incurred in preserving the item, not a reward, but reimbursement for costs like care or storage. Keep something you know belongs to someone else, though, and you cross into Alabama's criminal code: Sections 13A-8-6 through 13A-8-8.1 create the crime of theft of lost property, graded by value, first degree above $2,500 and lower degrees for smaller amounts.

That combination, a civil duty to deal honestly with found property and a criminal statute punishing those who do not, shapes how police, airports, and venues across the state handle a lost wallet, phone, or bag. Cities also run their own timelines, Alabama Code Section 11-47-116 holds unclaimed municipal proceeds for six months before conversion, and the state Treasury's Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act mails a notice to the apparent owner within 12 months of receiving property it holds. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Lost or Unclaimed Property, Ala. Code § 35-12-3
law.body: Alabama's civil code addresses found property directly. A finder is not obligated to take charge of lost items, but if they do, they are entitled to compensation for expenses necessarily incurred in preserving the property, not a discretionary reward. This is the legal backbone for how finders and owners are expected to deal with each other before a reward is even discussed.

law.title: Theft of Lost Property, Ala. Code §§ 13A-8-6 to 13A-8-8.1
law.body: It is a criminal offense in Alabama to actively obtain or exert control over property you know was lost or mislaid, without making reasonable efforts to return it. The charge is graded by value, exceeding $2,500 is theft of lost property in the first degree, and smaller amounts above $500 fall into lower degrees, so keeping a found item that clearly belongs to someone else can carry real consequences.

law.title: Municipal holding period, Ala. Code § 11-47-116
law.body: When a city or town in Alabama ends up holding property or its proceeds, the code requires those proceeds be held for six months for the account of the owner before they can be converted to municipal use. This is the kind of local clock that varies by department but has a baseline in state law.

law.title: State Treasury Unclaimed Property Act
law.body: Alabama's Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act, administered by the State Treasurer, requires a postcard notice be mailed to the apparent owner within 12 months of the Treasury receiving unclaimed property. This mainly covers financial assets and valuables that escheat to the state, separate from the everyday lost wallet or phone a local police department handles.

AL.whereTitle: Where items end up in Alabama
AL.whereBody: A lost item in Alabama might pass through Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport, Huntsville International Airport, Montgomery Regional Airport, or Mobile Regional Airport, through transit systems like the Birmingham-Jefferson County Transit Authority, or through university campuses such as the University of Alabama and Auburn, football stadiums, the Robert Trent Jones Golf Trail, or the beaches of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach. Each of these runs its own lost and found separate from city police departments. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: What happens if I keep something I found in Alabama?
faq.a: You could be charged under Alabama's theft of lost property statutes, Ala. Code §§ 13A-8-6 through 13A-8-8.1. If you know the item was lost and you exert control over it instead of trying to return it, the degree of the charge depends on its value, over $2,500 is first degree, over $500 is a lower degree. Turning it in to police or making a genuine effort to find the owner avoids all of this.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Departments typically ask for a description that includes one detail only the true owner would know, a serial number, a photo stored on the device, or something inside a bag, before releasing it to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Alabama?
faq.a: No. Alabama Code § 35-12-3 entitles a finder to reimbursement for expenses they necessarily incurred preserving the property, that is not the same as a mandatory reward. Offering one is always your choice, never a legal requirement to get your item back.

faq.q: How long will Alabama hold my property before it's disposed of?
faq.a: It depends on who is holding it. Municipal proceeds are held six months for the owner under Ala. Code § 11-47-116 before conversion. Property that escheats to the State Treasury under the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act gets a postcard notice within 12 months of receipt. Individual police departments and venues often set their own shorter windows, so checking directly matters.

faq.q: What if I lost something at an airport, stadium, or beach in Alabama?
faq.a: Airports, transit agencies, universities, and venues like the Gulf Shores beaches each run their own lost and found, separate from city police. ReportLost identifies the right one for the location you lost your item and files with them directly, alongside the local department.

AL.disclaimer: This page provides general information about Alabama law as of publication and is not legal advice. Procedures vary by city and department; verify details with your local authorities.

intro: If you lose something in Alaska, from a phone left on the Alaska Marine Highway ferry to a wallet dropped at a Fairbanks gas station, the state actually has something many states lack: a real statute that spells out what a finder is supposed to do with your property, and what happens if they don't do it.

Alaska Statutes Title 12 tells a finder to turn property over to a law enforcement agency and sets a one year clock before that finder can ever claim it as their own. Alaska Statutes Title 11 backs that up with a criminal charge for anyone who knowingly pockets lost or mislaid property instead. On top of that statewide framework, each city, from Anchorage to Juneau to Fairbanks, runs its own police property room with its own local holding periods. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: AS 12.36.045, When the Finder Becomes the Owner
law.body: Alaska's civil code says that when a private person finds property that is lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, delivering it to a law enforcement agency is the required step. If the true owner remains unknown or does not claim the property within one year, the finder can become the owner. That one year window is longer than the holding period in most states, which is good news if you are slow to file a report.

law.title: AS 11.46.160, Theft of Lost or Mislaid Property
law.body: Alaska criminal law makes it a crime, not just bad manners, to keep something you know belongs to someone else because it was lost, mislaid, or delivered to you by mistake. This is the statute Alaska police departments point to when they remind the public that finders keepers is not actually the law here.

law.title: Local Holding Periods Set the Real Clock
law.body: Underneath the state statute, individual departments run their own property rooms with their own timelines. Juneau Police Department holds unclaimed property for 90 days and unclaimed money for 6 months, with a written notice required if a finder wants to claim it. Anchorage Police Department can hold property anywhere from 10 days to 50 years or longer depending on the type of case, municipal code, and other legal holds involved. Always check with the specific department handling your item.

law.title: State Unclaimed Property Program (AS 34.45.280)
law.body: Separate from police lost and found, Alaska's Department of Revenue runs a statewide unclaimed property program for things like uncashed checks, dormant accounts, and other holder-reported property. Holders must file by November 1 each year for property held as of the prior June 30, and dormancy periods run from 1 to 15 years depending on the property type, with due diligence notices required once a property's value reaches 100 dollars.

AK.whereTitle: Where items end up in Alaska
AK.whereBody: Lost items in Alaska tend to surface through a small number of predictable channels: Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport, Fairbanks International Airport, and Juneau International Airport lost and found offices, the Alaska Marine Highway System ferries that connect coastal communities, cruise ship terminals during the summer season, local transit like Anchorage's People Mover and Juneau's Capital Transit, and city police department property rooms in Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Juneau. Hotels, museums, and rideshare drivers round out the rest. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, if you can prove it is yours. Departments typically ask you to describe the item and provide one detail only the true owner would know, like a specific mark, a photo stored on the phone, or what is inside a bag, before releasing it to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Alaska?
faq.a: No. Alaska law does not require you to pay a reward for the return of lost property. Offering one is always your choice, not a legal obligation.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps my lost item instead of turning it in?
faq.a: Under AS 11.46.160, a person who knowingly keeps property they know is lost or mislaid can be charged with theft of lost or mislaid property. Reporting the loss promptly to police creates a record that matters if this comes up later.

faq.q: How long will Alaska police hold my item before it's disposed of?
faq.a: It depends on the department. Juneau holds property for 90 days and cash for 6 months. Anchorage can hold items anywhere from 10 days to 50 years depending on the case. Statewide, AS 12.36.045 gives a finder up to one year before they can claim unclaimed property as their own, so you generally have time, but check with the specific department that has your item.

faq.q: What if my lost cash or property ends up reported to the state instead of a police department?
faq.a: Financial property like uncashed checks or dormant funds can end up with Alaska's Unclaimed Property Division rather than a police property room. Dormancy periods there run from 1 to 15 years depending on the property type, and you can search and claim through the state's unclaimed property program.

intro: Arkansas has no single statewide statute that tells a stranger what to do with your dropped phone or backpack. There is no Arkansas version of California's Civil Code lost property sections. What Arkansas does have is a criminal law that makes it illegal to knowingly keep something you find once you realize it belongs to someone else, plus a separate state system for unclaimed financial property, and a patchwork of city police department policies for physical items turned in at the counter.

That gap between criminal law and everyday practice is where most lost items actually get resolved, city by city, department by department. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Common law governs physical lost property
law.body: Arkansas has not enacted a dedicated lost-and-found statute covering ordinary found items like wallets, phones, or bags. Ownership and finder obligations for that kind of property are governed by common law principles: the true owner keeps legal title, and a finder does not automatically get to keep what they pick up.

law.title: Ark. Code § 5-36-105, theft of lost or mislaid property
law.body: Arkansas criminal law directly addresses this situation. A person who comes into control of property they know or should know is lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, and fails to take reasonable measures to return it to the owner, can be charged with theft under Ark. Code § 5-36-105. It is a Class D felony if the property is worth $1,000 or more, and a misdemeanor below that.

law.title: City police departments hold found items locally
law.body: Most Arkansas police departments, including in Little Rock, Fayetteville, and Fort Smith, accept found property at a records or property division and log it for a holding period set by local policy before unclaimed items are disposed of or auctioned. There is no single statewide holding period, so the timeline depends on which department has your item.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act covers money, not backpacks
law.body: Arkansas Code Title 18, Chapter 28 creates the Unclaimed Property Act, run by the Arkansas Auditor of State. It applies to financial property such as bank accounts, uncashed checks, and stock, not physical items lost in public. Holders must send a due diligence notice giving owners at least 90 days to respond, and property generally becomes reportable as abandoned three to seven years after it goes dormant.

law.title: No fixed statewide clock for physical items
law.body: Because there is no dedicated statute for found personal property, how long a department keeps your item before it is released, auctioned, or donated depends on that city's own rules, not a single Arkansas deadline. This is exactly why continuous, city-specific follow up matters more in Arkansas than in states with a set statutory holding period.

AR.whereTitle: Where items end up in Arkansas
AR.whereBody: Lost items in Arkansas typically surface at one of a few predictable points: Clinton National Airport in Little Rock, Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA), or Fort Smith Regional Airport if you were traveling; Rock Region Metro or Ozark Regional Transit if you were on a bus; and venue lost and found desks at places like Walton Arena, the Walmart AMP, Oaklawn in Hot Springs, or Razorback Stadium if you were at an event. Restaurants, hotels, and retail stores each keep their own found-item box or drawer, separate from any city system. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, if it was turned in to a police department, transit agency, airport, or venue, you can generally reclaim it once you prove ownership. That usually means describing the item accurately and providing one private verification detail, such as a passcode, a specific mark, or the contents of a bag, that only the real owner would know.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Arkansas?
faq.a: No. Arkansas has no statute requiring a reward for the return of lost property. Offering one is always your choice, never a legal obligation, and most items are returned without any reward changing hands.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps my lost item instead of turning it in?
faq.a: Arkansas criminal law addresses this directly. Under Ark. Code § 5-36-105, a person who knowingly keeps property they realize is lost or mislaid, without making a reasonable effort to return it, can be charged with theft, a Class D felony if the item is worth $1,000 or more.

faq.q: Is there a state deadline before my item is sold or disposed of?
faq.a: There is no single statewide deadline for physical lost items. Each Arkansas police department or venue sets its own holding period before unclaimed property is auctioned or donated. A separate rule applies to unclaimed financial property under the Unclaimed Property Act, which generally becomes reportable three to seven years after it goes dormant.

faq.q: What about lost cash, checks, or financial property specifically?
faq.a: That is a different track from a dropped wallet or phone. Uncashed checks, forgotten accounts, and similar financial property fall under the Arkansas Unclaimed Property Act, administered by the Auditor of State. You can search for and claim that kind of property directly through the state's ClaimItAR system.

AR.disclaimer: This page provides general information about Arkansas law as of publication and is not legal advice. Procedures vary by city and department; verify details with your local authorities.

intro: Colorado does not have one statewide lost and found statute that covers every city the way some states do. Instead, what happens to your lost item depends on which police department or agency picked it up. Denver, Northglenn, Pueblo, Weld County, Rangely and college campuses like Colorado State University each run their own found property ordinance, with their own claim windows and notice rules. The one statewide law that touches lost items directly is Colorado Revised Statutes 18-4-405, which says property obtained through theft must be restored to its owner regardless of who currently holds it.

There is also a completely separate system, the Colorado Unclaimed Property Program run by the State Treasurer, but that handles dormant financial accounts and business holdings, not the phone you left at a restaurant or the bag you left on the bus. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: No single statewide lost property statute, but CRS 18-4-405 protects owners
law.body: Colorado Revised Statutes 18-4-405 states that property obtained by theft, robbery or burglary must be restored to its owner and that no sale can cut off the true owner's right to it. This backs up your claim if a found item resurfaces through a pawnshop, private sale or resale platform, but it does not set out a finder's duty to turn property in. That job falls to city and county ordinances.

law.title: City and county ordinances actually run the process
law.body: Municipal codes like Northglenn's Article 6-14 Disposition of Personal Property, Pueblo's Chapter 4.32 Lost and Abandoned Property, Weld County's Charter and County Code, and the Town of Rangely's Police Property ordinance each spell out how a local department logs, holds, notifies and eventually disposes of found items. Which ordinance applies depends entirely on which department took custody of your item.

law.title: Claim windows differ by department
law.body: Under Northglenn's ordinance a written claim generally must come in within a 30 day claim period after notice, Pueblo treats property as abandoned 30 days after written notice is sent to the owner's last known address, Rangely requires the claimant to appear no less than 60 days after the item was surrendered, and Colorado State University's police policy holds found property and safekeeping property for a minimum of 90 days. There is no single statewide clock, so the department that has your item controls the deadline.

law.title: Colorado's Unclaimed Property Program is a different system
law.body: The Colorado Unclaimed Property Program, run through the State Treasurer, holds dormant financial property such as bank accounts, checks and business holdings valued at $25 or more, and companies must report and remit by November 1 each year. It exists to reunite people with forgotten financial assets, not with a lost wallet, phone or bag, which stays under local police or venue lost and found rules instead.

CO.whereTitle: Where items end up in Colorado
CO.whereBody: Lost property in Colorado moves through a lot of different hands depending on where you were. Denver International Airport and Colorado Springs Airport each run their own lost and found desks for items left at security, gates or baggage claim. RTD, Denver's regional transit agency, along with Bustang intercity buses, log items found on buses, light rail and at stations. City police departments, from Denver PD to smaller departments like Northglenn, Pueblo and Rangely, take custody of items found in public and on private property when a finder turns them in. College campuses such as Colorado State University run their own police property units, and major venues like Coors Field, Ball Arena, Red Rocks Amphitheatre and ski resorts across the state hold items separately under their own house policies. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Colorado departments generally will not hand an item over on a description alone, especially once a formal claim period has opened under a city ordinance. Be ready to describe a private detail that would not be obvious from looking at the item, such as a lock screen photo, a case scratch in a specific spot, or what is saved inside a bag pocket, along with matching ID if the department asks for it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Colorado?
faq.a: No. Colorado law does not require you to offer a reward to get your property back, and no ordinance in the search results sets a mandatory reward rule. Any reward is entirely your choice, and it can help motivate a faster return, but it is never a legal condition for getting your item back.

faq.q: How long will a Colorado police department hold my found item?
faq.a: It depends on which department has it. Some cities, like Northglenn, work off a 30 day claim window after written notice, Rangely gives claimants at least 60 days, and Colorado State University's campus police hold items for a minimum of 90 days. There is no one statewide holding period, so check with the specific department or let ReportLost confirm it for you.

faq.q: What happens if nobody claims my lost item in Colorado?
faq.a: Once the local claim period runs out without a valid claim, most Colorado ordinances allow the department to treat the item as abandoned. From there it may be sold, donated, destroyed, or in the case of unclaimed currency handled under the city's own rule, such as Northglenn's threshold for found currency of $100 or more. The exact outcome depends on the ordinance in the city that has your item.

faq.q: Do I have to turn in something I find in Colorado?
faq.a: Local ordinances in cities like Northglenn and Pueblo direct finders to report or hand over found property to the police department or another designated custodian rather than keep it. Holding onto something you know belongs to another person can also expose you to Colorado's theft statutes, since CRS 18-4-405 confirms that the true owner's right to stolen or improperly kept property is never cut off.

intro: Connecticut is one of the few states with a dedicated lost property statute still on the books. Connecticut General Statutes Chapter 859, Section 50-10, spells out exactly what a finder has to do: if you pick up an article worth a dollar or more, you are required to report it to the police department. That single sentence, unchanged for decades, is the backbone of how lost and found works across every city and town in the state.

From there, local police departments in Hartford, New Haven, Stamford, Bridgeport and every other municipality carry out the actual holding, logging and, if nobody claims it, disposal of found items. Separately, Connecticut's Treasurer runs a much larger system for unclaimed financial property like old bank accounts and uncashed checks through CTBiglist.gov, but that program is not where your lost phone or backpack ends up. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Duty to report (CGS § 50-10)
law.body: Anyone who finds and takes possession of an article worth one dollar or more is legally required to report the find to the police department. This is not optional courtesy, it is written into Chapter 859 of the state statutes, and it is the reason honest finders in Connecticut usually end up at a police station rather than keeping an item quietly.

law.title: Six month holding period
law.body: Once a police department receives a found article, Chapter 859 gives the original owner six months from that receipt date to come forward and claim it. If nobody claims it within that window, the department has two weeks after the deadline to move the property along, typically toward disposal or sale, so timing your report matters.

law.title: Larceny for keeping what you know isn't yours (CGS § 53a-119(4))
law.body: Connecticut's penal code folds lost and mislaid property directly into its larceny statute. Knowingly holding onto property you understand to be lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, instead of trying to return it or turning it in, can be charged as larceny, not just an ethical lapse.

law.title: State Treasurer's unclaimed property program
law.body: Separate from physical lost and found, Connecticut's Treasurer holds unclaimed financial property, old checks, dormant accounts and similar assets, through the CTBiglist.gov system, generally presumed abandoned after three or more years and payable within 90 days once a claim under CGS § 3-70a is verified. This is a different track from a lost wallet or phone, but it is worth checking if you are owed money you forgot about.

law.title: Local department and venue policies fill in the rest
law.body: Airports, transit agencies, stadiums and stores in Connecticut are not bound by Chapter 859's exact procedures, but they generally funnel found items to the nearest police department or their own lost and found desk, following the same spirit of holding items for the owner before disposing of them.

CT.whereTitle: Where items end up in Connecticut
CT.whereBody: Lost items in Connecticut tend to surface at a handful of predictable places. Bradley International Airport near Hartford and Tweed New Haven Airport both run their own lost and found operations for anything left at security, gates or baggage claim. CTtransit buses, Metro-North Railroad and Shore Line East trains each have separate lost and found contacts, since a phone left on a New Haven line train does not go to the same office as one left on a Hartford city bus. Large venues like Foxwoods Resort Casino, Mohegan Sun, the XL Center and Yale's athletic facilities keep their own logs for items left behind by visitors. Outside of these transit and venue systems, most found property in Connecticut cities and towns is reported directly to the local police department under Section 50-10. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: What happens if I find something worth more than a dollar in Connecticut?
faq.a: Under CGS § 50-10, you are required to report the find to the police department. This applies to any article valued at a dollar or more, which in practice covers almost everything from wallets and phones to jewelry.

faq.q: How long does a Connecticut police department hold a found item before it moves on?
faq.a: Chapter 859 gives the owner six months from the date the police department receives the item to come forward and claim it. If that period passes with no claim, the department has two weeks to dispose of the property, so reporting early gives you the best chance.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Departments typically ask for a private detail only the true owner would know, like a specific mark, a passcode, or the contents of a bag, before releasing the item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Connecticut?
faq.a: No. Offering a reward is always your choice, not a legal requirement under Connecticut law. Some people offer one to encourage a faster return, but nothing in the statute obligates it.

faq.q: Can I get in trouble for keeping something I found instead of reporting it?
faq.a: Yes. Connecticut's larceny statute, CGS § 53a-119(4), specifically covers acquiring property you know to have been lost or mislaid and treats knowingly keeping it as a form of theft, separate from the finder's duty to report under Section 50-10.

intro: Delaware does not have a single, dedicated lost and found statute like some larger states. Instead, the state's approach to a lost wallet, phone, or bag is built from two different pieces of law: a criminal statute that makes it theft to knowingly keep someone else's lost or mislaid property, and a separate statute telling state police what to do with property that ends up in their custody. Everything else, from a coffee shop's lost and found box to a casino's security office, runs on internal policy rather than a state mandate.
ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: No single statewide finder statute
law.body: Delaware has not enacted a standalone civil code section spelling out what a finder must do with lost property, the kind of statute some other states have. What exists instead is a criminal rule about keeping what is not yours, and a rule about what happens to property police are already holding, described below.

law.title: 11 Del. Code § 842, theft of lost or mislaid property
law.body: Delaware's theft statute directly addresses this situation: a person commits theft when they come into control of lost or mislaid property and, knowing who the owner is or how to find out, keeps it with intent to deprive them of it, instead of taking reasonable steps to return it. Under Title 11's theft grading, this is a class A misdemeanor if the property is worth less than $1,500, and rises to a class G felony at $1,500 or more.

law.title: 29 Del. Code § 8026, property held by the Department
law.body: When the Delaware State Police or another state department ends up holding lost, abandoned, or stolen property, this statute governs how it is handled if the owner cannot be located or does not come forward to claim it, including the eventual disposition of the item.

law.title: Local department and venue policy fills the rest
law.body: How long a Wilmington precinct, a beach town police desk, or a shopping mall security office holds an item, and what paperwork you need to get it back, is set by that department or business rather than by state law, so the exact process depends on where the item was found.

DE.whereTitle: Where items end up in Delaware
DE.whereBody: Lost items in Delaware tend to land in a handful of predictable places: local police departments in cities like Wilmington, Dover, and Newark, DART First State buses and stations, the Wilmington Amtrak and SEPTA rail station, New Castle Airport and Wilmington Airport, the Rehoboth Beach and Dewey Beach boardwalk area, Dover International Speedway and Dover Downs Hotel and Casino, and University of Delaware campus buildings. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you will need to prove it is yours. Departments and venues generally ask for a description that includes at least one private detail, such as a passcode, a specific mark, or what is inside a bag, before releasing the item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Delaware?
faq.a: No. Delaware law does not require finders or owners to offer a reward. Offering one is always your choice, and it can help encourage a faster return, but it is never legally owed.

faq.q: Is it actually a crime to keep a lost phone or wallet I found in Delaware?
faq.a: Yes. Under 11 Del. Code § 842, keeping lost or mislaid property when you know or could find out who the owner is, instead of taking reasonable steps to return it, is theft. Depending on the value, that can be charged as a misdemeanor or, at $1,500 or more, a felony.

faq.q: How long will Delaware police hold my item before it is disposed of?
faq.a: There is no single statewide holding period written into Delaware law for ordinary lost personal property. State police handle disposition of property in their custody under 29 Del. Code § 8026, but the practical timeline, notices, and claim window are set by each department, so you should confirm directly with the department holding your item.

faq.q: What if my lost item was actually left in a store or rented space rather than turned in to police?
faq.a: Businesses, landlords, and venues typically log items in an internal lost and found rather than sending them straight to police, and hold them for a period set by their own policy. Filing a report helps because it lets us alert those specific locations on your behalf, in addition to any relevant department.

intro: Hawaii is one of the few states where lost property is not left to guesswork. The legislature actually wrote down what a finder has to do, how long the police have to hold an item, and what happens if nobody claims it. Chapter 52D of the Hawaii Revised Statutes spells out the duty of finders, and a companion rule in Title 8 of the Hawaii Administrative Rules tells the county police departments exactly how many days to hold something before it can be released or disposed of.

Because the islands run on county government rather than one statewide police force, the department you deal with depends on where you lost the item, the Honolulu Police Department on Oahu, Maui Police, Hawaii Police on the Big Island, or Kauai Police. Add in a huge volume of visitors moving through airports, resorts, beaches, and rental cars, and the practical challenge is less about the law and more about knowing who to call first. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Duty and right of finders, HRS §52D-14
law.body: Under Hawaii Revised Statutes section 52D-14, anyone who finds money or property must report or deliver it to the chief of police of the county where it was found. This is a statutory duty, not just a suggestion, and it applies across all four counties.

law.title: The 45 day holding period
law.body: Once turned in, the property is held by the chief of police for forty five days, or until someone claiming it establishes title or right of custody. Hawaii Administrative Rules section 8-50-3 confirms that if no owner comes forward and establishes a claim, the item is returned to the finder after that forty five day window closes.

law.title: Keeping lost or mislaid property can be theft, HRS §708-830
law.body: Hawaii's theft statute, section 708-830, makes it a crime to knowingly obtain or exert unauthorized control over property you know to have been lost or mislaid. This is why the state pushes finders toward the police department rather than letting them decide on their own to keep something valuable.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Program, HRS Chapter 523A
law.body: When property or funds are held by a business, bank, or institution rather than found on the street, Hawaii's separate unclaimed property law takes over. The Department of Budget and Finance administers this program under Chapter 523A, and for smaller unclaimed funds under one hundred dollars, Act 184 requires the claim to be made within ten years of the deposit into the trust fund.

law.title: Venue specific rules, HRS §109-8
law.body: Hawaii even legislates lost and found at specific venues. Under section 109-8, money or property found at the stadium must be reported or delivered to stadium officials and is held for forty five days, mirroring the general finder statute. It is a reminder that in Hawaii, the rules can vary by the exact location where you lost something.

HI.whereTitle: Where items end up in Hawaii
HI.whereBody: Losses on Oahu often route through Daniel K. Inouye International Airport, TheBus system, Honolulu rideshares, hotels in Waikiki, or the Honolulu Police Department's found property desk. On Maui, Kahului Airport and resort lost and found offices are common stops, while the Big Island funnels through Ellison Onizuka Kona International or Hilo, and Kauai centers on Lihue Airport. Beaches, tour boats, luaus, and rental car counters across all four islands are frequent places where visitors realize something is missing. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to establish title or right of custody as HRS §52D-14 requires. In practice this means describing the item with one private detail that was not visible or listed publicly, such as what is stored inside a bag pocket or a specific mark on the item, so the county police department can confirm you are the true owner before releasing it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Hawaii?
faq.a: No. Nothing in Hawaii's finder statute or theft law requires you to pay a reward to get your property back. Offering one is always your choice, and many people do it informally to thank a finder, but it is never a legal condition of recovery.

faq.q: What happens if nobody claims my lost item within 45 days?
faq.a: Under Hawaii Administrative Rules section 8-50-3, if no owner establishes a claim within the forty five day holding period set by HRS §52D-14, the property is returned to the person who found it. This is why reporting a loss quickly matters, since the clock is already running once an item reaches the police.

faq.q: Which police department do I contact if I lost something on a different island?
faq.a: Hawaii does not have one statewide lost and found desk. Oahu losses go through the Honolulu Police Department, Maui through Maui Police, the Big Island through Hawaii Police, and Kauai through Kauai Police. Each county holds and processes found property under the same forty five day rule, but through its own department.

faq.q: What if I lost something at the airport or on a tour?
faq.a: Airports, tour operators, and venues like the stadium under HRS §109-8 often keep their own lost and found separate from the county police, at least for the first days after a loss. It is worth checking both the venue and the county police department, since unclaimed items are frequently turned over once the venue's own holding period ends.

intro: Washington DC runs its lost and found through the Metropolitan Police Department's Property Clerk system, a real statute most states its size do not have. D.C. Code § 5-119.02 gives police custody over property that is lost, stolen, or abandoned within the District, and a companion section, § 5-119.18, spells out what happens when nobody comes to claim it. MPD's Evidence Control Division then holds recovered items for a minimum of 180 days while it tries to track down the owner, after which unclaimed property is advertised and can be disposed of.

This is a different track from the DC Office of Finance's Unclaimed Property program, which handles dormant bank accounts, uncashed checks, and other financial assets under the Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act of 2021, not the phone you left on the Metro or the bag you left at a museum. Knowing which system your item falls under matters, because searching the wrong database wastes the days you have to act. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Property Clerk custody (D.C. Code § 5-119.02)
law.body: Any property that is lost, stolen, or believed to be feloniously obtained and recovered within the District is taken into the custody of the Metropolitan Police Property Clerk, not held informally by whichever officer or station happened to find it. This centralizes lost and found intake across the city into one system.

law.title: Minimum 180 day holding period
law.body: MPD's Evidence Control Division holds found and unattended property for a minimum of 180 days while it works to locate the rightful owner. Property that stays unclaimed past that window is treated as abandoned under § 5-119.18 and can be advertised and disposed of by the department.

law.title: Theft and receiving stolen property (D.C. Code §§ 22-3211, 22-3232)
law.body: D.C.'s general theft statute makes it a crime to wrongfully obtain or use another person's property with intent to deprive them of it, which covers someone who finds an item and simply keeps it. Knowingly receiving or holding onto property known to be stolen is a separate offense under § 22-3232, punishable by a fine under § 22-3571.01 or up to 180 days imprisonment.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act is a separate track
law.body: The Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act of 2021, administered by the DC Office of Finance, governs dormant financial property like uncashed checks and inactive accounts, generally presumed abandoned after three years and reportable at $50 or more. It is custodial with no deadline to claim, but it does not cover a lost wallet, bag, or phone, those go through MPD's Property Clerk process instead.

law.title: Court limits on how long police can hold items
law.body: DC's appeals court has ruled that police cannot hold a person's personal property for an unreasonable amount of time once it is no longer needed as evidence, reinforcing that the 180 day minimum is a floor for locating owners, not an open-ended excuse to keep items indefinitely.

DC.whereTitle: Where items end up in District of Columbia
DC.whereBody: Items lost around the National Mall, Smithsonian museums, and Capitol Hill often route to MPD's Property Clerk, while anything left on WMATA's Metrorail or Metrobus system goes through Metro Transit Police lost and found. Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) both run their own lost and found desks separate from city police, and hotels, Union Station, and event venues around the District typically hold items briefly before turning them over to local authorities. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you need to prove it is yours. MPD's Property Clerk will typically ask for a description that includes a private detail, like a specific mark, a saved contact, or a serial number, that would not be obvious to someone who simply found the item.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in District of Columbia?
faq.a: No. Offering a reward is always your choice, not a legal requirement anywhere in DC's lost property statutes. Some people offer one to encourage a faster return, but MPD and transit lost and found offices do not require it.

faq.q: How long does MPD hold found property before it's considered abandoned?
faq.a: D.C.'s Evidence Control Division holds recovered property for a minimum of 180 days while attempting to locate the owner. After that, under § 5-119.18, unclaimed items are advertised as abandoned and may be disposed of, so it pays to file a report as soon as possible.

faq.q: Should I search DC's Unclaimed Property website for my lost bag or phone?
faq.a: No, that database is for financial assets like old bank accounts and uncashed checks under the Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act. A lost personal item recovered in the city goes through MPD's Property Clerk system instead, not the Office of Finance's unclaimed money search.

faq.q: What happens if I don't report my item lost right away?
faq.a: The clock on MPD's 180 day holding period starts running as soon as an item is logged as found, whether or not you've reported it missing. Waiting to report only shortens your realistic window to match with an item before it can be treated as abandoned.

intro: Idaho actually has a statewide statute for this, which puts it in a different category than states that rely only on common law. Idaho Code Title 55 tells sheriffs and city police departments what to do with abandoned or unclaimed property that comes into their custody, including selling it at public auction once the holding period runs out. Idaho's criminal code goes a step further than most states by spelling out, in the theft statute itself, that keeping something you know was lost or mislaid by someone else is theft, not finders keepers.

What Idaho does not do is set one statewide clock for how long a police department must hold your wallet, phone, or bag before it can be disposed of. That is left to each city. Moscow gives a finder thirty days before the item is released to them if unclaimed. Fruitland holds property for six months. Spirit Lake holds found property for one hundred eighty days before disposing of it. So the practical answer to how long you have to claim something in Idaho depends on which police department picked it up. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Idaho Code § 55-403, Property in General
law.body: This statute authorizes sheriffs and city police departments to take custody of abandoned or unclaimed property and, after the applicable holding period, sell it at public auction. It is the legal basis local departments in Idaho point to when they eventually clear out a found property room.

law.title: Local holding periods set by city ordinance
law.body: Idaho does not fix one statewide number of days. Moscow's municipal code gives a finder thirty days to claim property before it can be released to them. Fruitland holds all found items for six months before auction or disposal. Spirit Lake's ordinance sets a one hundred eighty day window. Which clock applies to your item depends on which department has it, which is why it matters that a report reaches the correct city desk.

law.title: Idaho Code § 18-2403, Theft
law.body: Idaho's theft statute explicitly defines acquiring lost property, stating a person commits theft when they exercise control over property they know to have been lost or mislaid and fail to take reasonable steps to return it. This gives police a direct criminal hook when someone pockets a found phone or wallet instead of turning it in.

law.title: Idaho State Treasurer, Unclaimed Property Division
law.body: Cash, accounts, and other financial property that goes unclaimed are handled separately under Idaho's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, with the Treasurer's office running the statewide database at yourmoney.idaho.gov. Holders generally must attempt to contact an owner before turning over property worth fifty dollars or more, but this track is for financial instruments, not the phone or backpack you left at a restaurant.

ID.whereTitle: Where items end up in Idaho
ID.whereBody: In the Boise area, lost items move through Boise Airport, Valley Regional Transit buses, Boise State's stadium and event venues, and downtown restaurants and hotels. In eastern Idaho, Idaho Falls Regional Airport and Pocatello Regional Airport have their own lost and found desks, and in the north, travelers often route through Spokane International Airport just across the state line. Ski resorts around Sun Valley and McCall, state parks, and university campuses each run their own found property process separate from city police departments. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Idaho departments typically ask for a description that includes at least one private verification detail, something like a specific mark, a passcode, or the contents of a bag, that would not be visible to the person who found it or to a stranger reading a lost report.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Idaho?
faq.a: No. Idaho law does not require finders to be paid, and nothing in the state's found property or theft statutes sets a mandatory reward. Offering one is always your choice, not a legal obligation.

faq.q: How long will the police hold my lost item in Idaho?
faq.a: It depends entirely on which city's department has it, since Idaho leaves the holding period to local ordinance. Moscow allows thirty days before releasing an unclaimed item to the finder, Fruitland holds items for six months, and Spirit Lake holds found property for one hundred eighty days before disposal.

faq.q: What happens if no one claims my lost item?
faq.a: Under Idaho Code § 55-403, once the local holding period expires, the police department or sheriff's office can sell the property at public auction. Some cities instead release it to the finder or donate it, depending on their own ordinance.

faq.q: Is keeping a lost item a crime in Idaho?
faq.a: It can be. Idaho Code § 18-2403 specifically defines theft to include acquiring lost or mislaid property when you know it was lost and do not make a reasonable effort to return it to the owner, so knowingly keeping someone's found phone or wallet is not a legal gray area here.

intro: Indiana does not hand every lost item to one clean statute the way a few states do. Instead the state splits the job three ways. Indiana State Police have their own code section for property that comes into an officer's hands as stolen, lost, or abandoned. Property connected to a criminal case follows a separate evidence statute with its own hold and destruction timeline. And anything that turns into unclaimed cash, deposits, or business-held funds falls under Indiana's Unclaimed Property Act, run out of the Attorney General's office, not the police department down the street.

For everyday items, a dropped phone at Gainbridge Fieldhouse, a bag left on an IndyGo bus, Indiana leans on old-fashioned common law duty to return plus whatever policy the individual police department, airport, or venue has posted, and Indiana courts have even ruled that simply taking money someone else lost is not automatically a crime under the state's theft statute. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Delivery of Stolen, Lost, and Abandoned Property (IC 10-11-5-2)
law.body: When money, goods, or other property that has been stolen, lost, or abandoned comes into the possession of an Indiana State Police employee, this section governs what happens to it next. It is the closest thing Indiana has to a dedicated state lost and found statute, but it applies to ISP custody, not to every city or county department, which each set their own intake and hold procedures.

law.title: Property Held as Evidence (IC 35-33-5-5)
law.body: Property connected to a criminal investigation follows a different timeline. Once the case concludes, the statute allows for disposition after ninety days, and property whose possession is unlawful can be destroyed sixty days after that. This is why an item recovered during a police report or investigation may take longer to get back than something simply turned in at a front desk.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act (IC 32-34-1.5)
law.body: Indiana's Unclaimed Property Division, run through the Attorney General's office at indianaunclaimed.gov, handles property held by businesses, banks, and other holders once it goes dormant. Holders must send due diligence mailings on property valued at fifty dollars or more, and unclaimed funds can be held by the state for years before they are considered permanently unclaimed. This track is mostly about money and accounts, not a dropped wallet or backpack.

law.title: Theft Statute and Case Law (IC 35-43-4-2)
law.body: Indiana's general theft statute makes it a Class A misdemeanor to knowingly exert unauthorized control over someone else's property, but the Indiana Court of Appeals ruled in 2020 that simply taking money that was lost or mislaid is not automatically a crime under this statute. Indiana has not enacted a separate 'theft of lost or mislaid property' offense the way some other states have, so intent and circumstances matter a great deal in how a finder's conduct is treated.

law.title: Local Department Found Property Policies
law.body: Below the state statutes, day to day lost and found work in Indiana runs through individual department policy. Westfield Police Department, for example, maintains its own found property list and requires callers to verify details by phone before pickup. Other cities, campuses, and transit agencies each keep their own logs, hold periods, and verification steps.

IN.whereTitle: Where items end up in Indiana
IN.whereBody: Lost items in Indiana tend to land with whoever was running the place you were in. Indianapolis International Airport, South Bend International Airport, Fort Wayne International Airport, and Evansville Regional Airport each keep their own lost and found desks separate from airline counters. IndyGo handles transit-related lost items in Indianapolis, while Indianapolis Metropolitan Police, county sheriffs, and smaller city departments like Westfield or Carmel each maintain their own found property intake. Large venues such as Lucas Oil Stadium, Gainbridge Fieldhouse, the Indiana State Fairgrounds, and the Indianapolis Motor Speedway typically hold items found on site before anything reaches a police department. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: What happens if no one claims my lost item in Indiana?
faq.a: It depends on who is holding it. Property in Indiana State Police custody follows IC 10-11-5-2, evidence property follows the ninety day and sixty day timeline in IC 35-33-5-5, and money or accounts held by businesses can escheat to the state's Unclaimed Property Division after a dormancy period. Ordinary found items, like a phone or a jacket, are usually handled under whatever hold period the local department or venue sets on its own.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you will need to prove it is yours. Departments and the Unclaimed Property Division both require identification, and for physical items you will typically also be asked for one private verification detail, such as a case color, a lock screen photo, or a serial number, that only the true owner would know before they release it to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Indiana?
faq.a: No. Indiana law does not require a reward for returning lost property. Offering one is always your choice, and plenty of items are returned in Indiana with no reward involved at all.

faq.q: Does Indiana have a specific lost and found statute?
faq.a: Not one single law covering every situation. Indiana State Police custody is covered by IC 10-11-5-2, evidence property by IC 35-33-5-5, and business-held unclaimed funds by the Unclaimed Property Act, but day to day found items at airports, transit agencies, and venues are governed by each department's own policy rather than one statewide lost and found statute.

faq.q: Is keeping a found item against the law in Indiana?
faq.a: It can be, but Indiana's theft statute is narrower here than in some states. Courts have held that simply taking money that was lost or mislaid is not automatically a crime under IC 35-43-4-2, though knowingly keeping an item after learning who owns it can still expose you to theft charges or civil liability depending on the facts, so turning it in to the local department is the safest move.

intro: Iowa is one of the few states with an actual lost property statute still on its books. Chapter 556F, the Lost Property Act, sets out what a finder is supposed to do with money, goods, bank notes, or anything else of value that turns up without an owner in sight, right down to a newspaper notice requirement for higher value items. That puts Iowa in a different category from states that rely only on common law or a general theft statute.

In practice, most day to day recoveries in Iowa run through city police department property and evidence units, which hold unclaimed items for a set period before disposing of them, alongside the statewide Great Iowa Treasure Hunt program that handles unclaimed financial property under Chapter 556. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Iowa's Lost Property Act (Chapter 556F)
law.body: Chapter 556F is Iowa's dedicated lost property statute. It covers any lost goods, money, bank notes, or other things of value and lays out what a finder must do to give the true owner a fair chance to reclaim the item, rather than leaving the matter to informal custom.

law.title: Newspaper notice for items over $40
law.body: Under Chapter 556F, if the found property is worth more than forty dollars, the finder is required to publish notice of the find once a week for three consecutive weeks in a local newspaper, so the owner has a documented chance to come forward.

law.title: Twelve month claim window
law.body: Once proof of the find has been given under Chapter 556F, the original owner generally has twelve months to appear and prove ownership. If nobody claims the property and proves ownership within that window, the statute allows the finder's claim to move forward.

law.title: Local police department holding periods
law.body: City departments handle most everyday lost and found turn ins separately from Chapter 556F. Departments such as Cedar Rapids and Clinton police hold property with an unknown owner for a ninety day period before it is disposed of, and other Iowa departments follow similar internal timelines.

law.title: Great Iowa Treasure Hunt and Chapter 556
law.body: Iowa's Treasurer of State runs the Great Iowa Treasure Hunt for unclaimed financial property, such as forgotten bank accounts, under Chapter 556, with a dormancy period of about three years for most property types. This track is separate from physical items lost in public places or businesses.

IA.whereTitle: Where items end up in Iowa
IA.whereBody: Lost items in Iowa typically surface at the place they were left, whether that is a Des Moines International Airport gate, the Eastern Iowa Airport in Cedar Rapids, a DART bus in Des Moines, a CyRide bus in Ames, a University of Iowa or Iowa State University building, a Wells Fargo Arena event, a Hy-Vee store, or a local casino floor. From there items get logged by venue staff or handed to the city police department's property and evidence unit under local policy. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, once you can prove it is yours. Departments and venues in Iowa typically ask for a description plus one detail only the owner would know, such as a specific mark, a saved photo on a phone, or the contents of a bag, before releasing it to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Iowa?
faq.a: No. Offering a reward is always your choice, not a legal requirement under Iowa law, though a modest reward can sometimes speed up a return.

faq.q: What happens if no one claims my lost item in Iowa?
faq.a: It depends on where it was turned in. Items handled under Chapter 556F may follow a formal notice and twelve month claim process for higher value finds, while items turned in to a city police department are usually held for around ninety days and then disposed of if the owner is unknown.

faq.q: How long does Iowa law require finders to hold onto property?
faq.a: Chapter 556F sets specific steps for finders, including publishing notice for items over forty dollars for three consecutive weeks and giving the owner up to twelve months to come forward with proof. Local police departments run their own separate holding periods, commonly about ninety days, for property turned in to them.

faq.q: Where should I report a lost item in Iowa?
faq.a: Start with the police department covering the city where you lost it, since that is where most finders and venues turn items in, and also contact the specific airport, transit agency, or business you visited. ReportLost sends your report to those local contacts on your behalf.

intro: Kansas does not have one statewide civil code section that spells out exactly what a store, airport, or transit agency must do with something you left behind. Instead, Kansas handles lost property mostly through its criminal code and through local city ordinances. The starting point is K.S.A. 21-5802, which makes it a crime to keep property you know is lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake once you know or can learn who the owner is.

Because there is no single statewide civil lost-and-found statute, the practical rules come from two places: the criminal theft statute that pressures finders to hand items over, and city-level ordinances (police department policies and municipal codes) that set holding periods and auction procedures for property that ends up in police custody. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Theft of lost or mislaid property, K.S.A. 21-5802
law.body: Kansas criminal law treats failing to take reasonable measures to return lost, mislaid, or misdelivered property to its owner as theft. Penalties scale with value: property worth $100,000 or more is a severity level 5 nonperson felony, at least $25,000 is a lower felony tier, and property valued under $1,000 is a class A nonperson misdemeanor. This statute is the main legal lever pushing finders in Kansas to turn items in rather than keep them.

law.title: City-set holding periods before disposal
law.body: Individual Kansas cities, not one state law, decide how long an item sits in police custody before it can be sold or disposed of. Beloit's municipal code, for example, requires unclaimed property to be held for a minimum of 90 days before public auction. Other Kansas cities set their own timelines in local code, so the exact wait depends on where the item was turned in.

law.title: Police department found-property policies
law.body: Kansas police departments run their own internal procedures for items found or turned in for safekeeping. The Kansas City, Kansas Police Department, for instance, has a written found, safekeeping, and evidentiary property policy directing officers to log and secure items as soon as they take possession. Smaller Kansas departments follow comparable local procedures rather than a single statewide rulebook.

law.title: Evidence held under K.S.A. 22-2512
law.body: If your lost item was seized in connection with a criminal case, K.S.A. 22-2512 allows police to keep it in custody for as long as it may be needed as evidence. Once no charges are filed or a prosecution is declined, the statute requires the property to be returned to its rightful owner or disposed of according to the same section.

law.title: State Treasurer's unclaimed property program
law.body: The Kansas State Treasurer administers a separate unclaimed property program for financial assets like uncashed checks, dormant accounts, and similar intangible property, generally using a dormancy period of around five years. This program is distinct from physical items lost at an airport, store, or transit stop, which stay under local police and city ordinance rules.

KS.whereTitle: Where items end up in Kansas
KS.whereBody: Lost items in Kansas typically surface at Kansas City International Airport (MCI), Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport, city bus systems like the Kansas City Area Transportation Authority, university campuses such as the University of Kansas and Kansas State University, and venues including Children's Mercy Park and Intrust Bank Arena. Each of these tends to run its own lost and found desk before anything reaches a police department's custody. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, once you prove it is yours. Kansas police departments and venue lost and found desks generally ask for a description plus one private verification detail, such as a specific mark, a saved photo on the device, or the contents of a bag, before releasing property to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Kansas?
faq.a: No. Kansas law does not require you to pay a reward to get your item back. Offering one is always your choice, and Kansas's theft-of-lost-property statute focuses on the finder's duty to return the item, not on any reward obligation from the owner.

faq.q: What happens if someone in Kansas just keeps what they found?
faq.a: It can be a crime. Under K.S.A. 21-5802, keeping property you know is lost or mislaid, once you know or can find out who owns it, is theft. The charge level depends on value, ranging from a class A nonperson misdemeanor for items under $1,000 up to a felony for higher-value property.

faq.q: How long will Kansas police hold my item before disposing of it?
faq.a: It depends on the city, since Kansas has no single statewide holding period for ordinary lost property. Some municipal codes, like Beloit's, set a 90-day minimum hold before public auction. Check with the specific department or city that has your item for its local timeline.

faq.q: What if my lost item was seized as evidence?
faq.a: If police kept your property because it relates to a criminal case, K.S.A. 22-2512 allows them to hold it as long as it may be needed for trial. Once charges are resolved or declined, the statute requires the property to be returned to you or disposed of under the same section.

intro: Kentucky doesn't have one statute that walks a finder through what to do with a lost phone or wallet. Instead, the state relies on a mix of criminal law that punishes keeping what isn't yours, local police property rooms that each set their own rules, and a separate State Treasury program for unclaimed financial assets like old bank accounts and uncashed checks.

That patchwork means your outcome depends heavily on which city you lost something in and which department ends up holding it. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: No statewide lost property statute, KRS 514.050 fills the gap
law.body: Kentucky has no single law spelling out what a finder must do with a lost wallet or phone. Instead, the criminal code addresses it through KRS 514.050, Theft of property lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, which makes it a crime to keep property you know isn't yours without taking reasonable steps to return it. It's a Class B misdemeanor unless the property is worth $500 or more, which pushes the charge higher.

law.title: Local police property units set the real timeline
law.body: Because state law doesn't fix a holding period for physical items, individual departments do. Lexington's Property and Evidence Unit, for example, holds found property for 90 days before it's released, auctioned, or otherwise disposed of. Louisville, Bowling Green, and other Kentucky cities run their own property rooms with their own intake and disposal rules, so the department holding your item is the one whose clock actually matters.

law.title: State Treasury handles unclaimed money, not lost objects
law.body: Kentucky's Unclaimed Property program, run by the State Treasury, is built for financial assets, dormant bank accounts, uncashed checks, stocks, insurance payouts, not a lost backpack or set of keys. Holders must turn over dormant accounts after a dormancy period of about three years, and the Treasury keeps those funds searchable with no deadline to claim them. A backpack left at a restaurant or on a TARC bus goes through the finder or the local police department, not the Treasury.

law.title: Finder's keepers is not a legal defense
law.body: A popular myth holds that finders can keep what they find. Kentucky law addresses this directly: keeping something you found while knowing it belongs to someone else is theft of property lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake under KRS 514.050. Turning an item over to police or making a genuine effort to locate the owner is what keeps a finder out of that exposure.

KY.whereTitle: Where items end up in Kentucky
KY.whereBody: Items go missing across Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport, and Blue Grass Airport in Lexington, on transit systems like TARC in Louisville and Lextran in Lexington, and at venues from Rupp Arena and Kentucky Speedway to the hotels, restaurants, and racetracks that draw crowds during Derby season. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you'll need to prove ownership. Departments typically ask you to describe the item and provide one detail only the true owner would know, like a passcode, a photo stored inside, or an engraving, before releasing it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Kentucky?
faq.a: No. Kentucky law doesn't require finders to be paid a reward for returning lost property. It's always your choice, though offering one can sometimes speed up a return.

faq.q: How long will Lexington or Louisville police hold my item?
faq.a: Lexington's Property and Evidence Unit holds found property for 90 days before disposing of it. Louisville and other Kentucky departments set their own windows, so it's worth calling the specific department directly to confirm.

faq.q: What happens if no one claims my lost item?
faq.a: After the local holding period ends, the department disposes of it per its own policy, which can mean auction, donation, or destruction. Unclaimed financial property instead moves to the State Treasury, which keeps it available to claim indefinitely.

faq.q: Can someone be charged with a crime for keeping what I lost?
faq.a: Yes. Under KRS 514.050, keeping lost, mislaid, or misdelivered property you know isn't yours is theft. It's a Class B misdemeanor unless the property is worth $500 or more, which raises the offense.

intro: Louisiana does not have one tidy lost and found statute the way a few other states do. What you get instead is a patchwork: a Civil Code and common law tradition that puts a duty on a finder to make a real effort to locate the owner, a criminal theft statute that turns keeping a lost item into a crime once you know it is not yours, and a set of Revised Statutes that tell police departments and sheriffs how long they must hold property before they can dispose of it. Which rule applies to your bag, phone, or ring depends on where it turned up and who has it now.

That patchwork matters in practice. A wallet handed to a French Quarter bar back gets logged under that business's own policy. A phone turned in at a NOPD district station falls under the 150 day holding rule in the Revised Statutes. A backpack seized as possible evidence during a police stop can sit under a different, one year rule while a criminal case plays out. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: No single lost property statute, common law duty applies
law.body: Unlike states with a dedicated Civil Code provision spelling out exactly what a finder must do, Louisiana leans on common law principles. A finder who picks up lost property is expected to make reasonable efforts to identify and notify the owner rather than simply keep it. There is no statewide form or waiting period built for this scenario, it is a background duty that shapes how honest finders and local departments are expected to act.

law.title: La. R.S. 33:2333: 150 day holding period for police departments
law.body: When noncontraband property is turned in to a municipal police department, the statute says it cannot be disposed of before 150 days have passed. If the owner has not claimed it by then, the department can move to dispose of it under the procedure set out in that section. That 150 day window is the closest thing Louisiana has to a statewide lost and found clock.

law.title: La. Code Crim. Proc. art. 228.3 and 228.4: property tied to investigations
law.body: Property seized in connection with a criminal investigation, rather than simply found and turned in, follows a different track. If it remains unclaimed and is not needed for any criminal proceeding, a sheriff may petition the court after the lapse of one year to dispose of it. This is the rule most likely to apply if your item was recovered during an arrest or a police stop rather than handed in at a counter.

law.title: La. R.S. 14:67: keeping lost property can be theft
law.body: Louisiana's theft statute covers the misappropriation of property you know belongs to someone else, which includes lost or mislaid items a finder decides to keep instead of trying to return. Penalties scale with value, misappropriation of less than one thousand dollars can carry up to six months in jail plus a fine, with steeper penalties as the value climbs. This is the legal backbone behind the duty to try to return what you find.

law.title: Local department policies fill in the rest
law.body: Outside of the 150 day and one year rules, cities and parishes set their own procedures for logging, storing, and releasing found property, and those procedures vary from New Orleans to Baton Rouge to Shreveport. Knowing which department has your item, and what its intake desk actually requires, matters as much as knowing the statute.

LA.whereTitle: Where items end up in Louisiana
LA.whereBody: In New Orleans, items go missing through Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport, on RTA buses and the St. Charles Avenue streetcar line, in the French Quarter's bars and hotels, and around the Superdome and Caesars Superdome event crowds. Baton Rouge routes lost property through Baton Rouge Metropolitan Airport and the Capital Area Transit System, while Shreveport, Lafayette, and other cities each have their own regional airport and transit lost and found desks plus casino and riverboat security offices. Mardi Gras season alone generates its own wave of reports from parade routes, French Quarter venues, and hotel lobbies. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, if you can show it is yours. Departments in Louisiana typically ask for a description plus one private detail only the owner would know, such as a lock screen photo, a serial number, or what is inside a bag's zip pocket. That detail is what separates a real owner from someone guessing.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Louisiana?
faq.a: No. Louisiana law does not require you to offer or pay a reward to get your property back. Offering one is always your choice, and it can sometimes speed things along, but no statute or department policy makes it mandatory.

faq.q: How long will police in Louisiana hold my lost item?
faq.a: For property turned in to a municipal police department, La. R.S. 33:2333 sets a minimum 150 day holding period before the department can dispose of unclaimed noncontraband property. Property tied to an active criminal case can be held longer, up to a year or more, under a separate rule in the Code of Criminal Procedure.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps my lost item instead of turning it in?
faq.a: Once a finder knows an item belongs to someone else and decides to keep it anyway, that can amount to theft under La. R.S. 14:67. Penalties depend on the value of the item, with misdemeanor level penalties for lower value property and steeper felony exposure as value rises.

faq.q: I lost something at Louis Armstrong airport or on a New Orleans streetcar, what do I do?
faq.a: Airport lost and found desks and RTA's transit lost and found handle these separately from NOPD, and each keeps its own log and holding timeline. File with ReportLost as soon as you notice the loss, since we send your report to the specific desk that matches where and how you traveled.
