intro: Maryland does not have one all-purpose lost property statute like some states. Instead, the rules around a found phone, wallet, or bag come from a mix of sources: a criminal statute that makes it illegal to knowingly keep something you know isn't yours, a courts and judicial proceedings law that governs how police release property once they have it, and individual policies set by each police department, from Baltimore to Easton to the Maryland Capitol Police.

That patchwork means a lot depends on which department ends up holding your item and what that department's own claim window looks like. A separate, unrelated track exists for unclaimed financial property, like uncashed checks or old bank accounts, held by the Comptroller's office indefinitely, but that is not the system that handles a backpack left on a MARC train or a phone turned in at BWI. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Criminal Law § 7-104, theft of lost or mislaid property
law.body: Maryland makes it a crime to obtain or keep control over property you know was lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, once you know who the owner is. Penalties scale with the value of the property, up to a felony charge at $100,000 or more. This is the legal backbone that discourages people from simply pocketing what they find.

law.title: Courts and Judicial Proceedings § 3-505, police custody and release
law.body: Once police take custody of property, the law requires notification to the owner, who then has up to 30 days to secure its release. This 30-day window is the closest thing Maryland has to a statewide found-property clock, though it governs the release process rather than setting one uniform holding period for every department.

law.title: Local department policies fill in the gaps
law.body: Beyond § 3-505, each department runs its own claim process. Baltimore Police generally requires scheduling an appointment with about 5 days lead time. Maryland Capitol Police policy calls for holding property roughly 10 days past the date listed on a notification letter. Smaller jurisdictions, like Easton, have their own municipal code sections covering custody and disposition of abandoned, lost, or seized property. Always check with the specific department holding your item.

law.title: Unclaimed property is a separate system
law.body: The Comptroller's Unclaimed Property program, searchable at claimitmd.gov, covers dormant financial assets like old bank accounts and uncashed checks reported by businesses. Maryland law treats this property as custodial, meaning there is no statute of limitations for the original owner or their heirs to claim it. It has nothing to do with a lost purse or laptop turned in to a police desk.

law.title: No fixed statewide hold time for evidence
law.body: When property is connected to an open investigation, Maryland courts have recognized that police can hold it as long as reasonably necessary, with no set statewide time limit. This can extend well beyond the 30-day release window that applies to ordinary found property once an investigation is involved.

MD.whereTitle: Where items end up in Maryland
MD.whereBody: Lost items in Maryland typically surface at a handful of predictable places: Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), MARC train stations and Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) buses and light rail, WMATA Metro stations for commuters in Montgomery and Prince George's counties, stadiums like Camden Yards and M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore, shopping centers, hotels, and beach boardwalks in Ocean City during summer travel season. Each of these has its own lost and found desk or contracted lost property vendor, separate from the police department property rooms described above. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, once you can prove ownership. Departments typically ask for a description that only the true owner would know, like a specific mark, a passcode, or what's inside a bag's inner pocket, before releasing the item under the § 3-505 process.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Maryland?
faq.a: No. Maryland law does not require a reward for the return of lost property. Offering one is always your choice, not a legal obligation.

faq.q: What happens if no one claims the item?
faq.a: Under § 3-505, the owner generally has up to 30 days after notification to claim property held by police. After that, disposition depends on the holding department's own policy, which can include auction, donation, or, in some departments, release to the finder.

faq.q: Can I get in trouble for keeping something I found?
faq.a: Yes. Criminal Law § 7-104 makes it a crime to knowingly keep property you know was lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, once the owner's identity is known. Penalties increase with the value of the item, up to felony charges for high-value property.

faq.q: How long will police hold my lost item?
faq.a: There is no single statewide number. Maryland courts have noted there's no fixed limit for property tied to an investigation, while ordinary found property is generally governed by the 30-day release window under § 3-505, and each department, from Baltimore to the Capitol Police, layers on its own appointment and hold procedures.

MD.disclaimer: This page provides general information about Maryland law as of publication and is not legal advice. Procedures vary by city and department, verify details with your local authorities.

intro: Massachusetts is one of the few states with a real, on the books statute for what a police department has to do with property someone hands in. General Law Chapter 135, Section 8 spells out the finder's duty, the reporting steps, and even a fine for a finder who ignores them. That gives Massachusetts a clearer paper trail than most states, at least on paper.

In practice, what happens to your phone, bag, or wallet after it is found in Boston, Worcester, or Springfield still depends heavily on which department picked it up and how that department's own property room policy works. Some hold items for a month, some for a year. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: The finder's duty statute, G.L. c. 135, §8
law.body: Massachusetts law requires a finder to report lost money or goods, and covers what a police department does with unclaimed property once it is turned in. A finder who does not comply can face a fine of not less than fifty dollars. This is the backbone of how a Massachusetts lost and found report actually gets handled once you file it with a department.

law.title: Holding periods vary by department
law.body: Chapter 135, Section 8 references a one month unclaimed period as a trigger point in the process, but individual departments set their own practical hold times on top of that. Marshfield Police, for example, holds found property for one year before it can become the property of the finder, and Wakefield's property unit describes a similar one year mark for private holders who file a timely report. Falmouth handles arrest related property differently, on a 30 day cycle. Always confirm the actual hold time with the department that has your item.

law.title: Larceny risk under G.L. c. 266, §30
law.body: Massachusetts larceny law covers stealing, embezzling, or converting someone else's personal property, and keeping something you know is not yours after finding it can fall under this statute rather than simple lost and found. Property valued under 250 dollars is typically charged as petty larceny, a misdemeanor, which is one more reason departments push finders to report rather than keep.

law.title: A separate track for money and financial property
law.body: Massachusetts also runs the Unclaimed Property Law under G.L. c. 200A, handled through the State Treasurer's findmassmoney.gov site. This covers abandoned bank accounts, uncashed checks, and similar financial property, not the phone you left on the T. It is a completely separate system from a police department's found property room, and it is worth checking if you are searching for money rather than a physical item.

MA.whereTitle: Where items end up in Massachusetts
MA.whereBody: Logan International Airport in Boston runs its own lost and found through Massport, separate from any city police department, and if your item was left on a plane the airline holds a different piece of it. The MBTA, covering the Boston subway, buses, and commuter rail, has its own transit lost and found process, and regional agencies elsewhere in the state run their own. Local police departments across Massachusetts, from Boston down to smaller cities and towns, hold found property under their own version of the Chapter 135 process. Big venues, museums, Fenway Park, TD Garden, and downtown retail districts each have their own house policies for anything left behind. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours before a Massachusetts police department or venue will release it. That usually means matching a serial number, showing a photo with metadata, or naming a specific detail about the item's contents or condition that only the owner would know. Departments hold found property specifically so they can verify this before handing anything over.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Massachusetts?
faq.a: No. Massachusetts law does not require a reward for returning lost property. Offering one is entirely up to you, and plenty of items get returned with nothing more than a thank you.

faq.q: How long will a Massachusetts police department hold my lost item?
faq.a: It depends on the department. Chapter 135, Section 8 sets a one month unclaimed mark as part of the legal process, but many departments hold property much longer in practice, Marshfield and Wakefield both point to roughly one year before unclaimed property can pass to the finder. Contact the specific department holding your item for its actual policy.

faq.q: What happens if someone finds my item and just keeps it?
faq.a: That can cross into larceny under G.L. c. 266, §30, which covers stealing or converting someone else's property, including property that was simply found rather than taken. Items worth under 250 dollars are typically charged as petty larceny, a misdemeanor, which is part of why Massachusetts law pushes finders to report rather than keep what they pick up.

faq.q: What if I am searching for lost money or a financial account, not a physical item?
faq.a: That falls under a different Massachusetts system entirely, the Unclaimed Property Law, G.L. c. 200A, run by the State Treasurer through findmassmoney.gov. It covers things like dormant bank accounts and uncashed checks, not physical items in a police department's property room, so it is worth checking separately if that is what you are missing.

MA.disclaimer: This page provides general information about Massachusetts law as of publication and is not legal advice. Procedures vary by city and department, verify details with your local authorities.

intro: Minnesota is one of the few states where lost property has its own statute instead of just a mash of city ordinances. Minnesota Statutes 345.15 and 345.16 spell out what happens when personal property turns up abandoned on a public way, sidewalk, or other public premises, including a sheriff's power to seize it, a minimum three month hold before it can be sold at public auction, and a 90 day window for the rightful owner to reclaim it after notice by paying any expenses incurred.

Cities and counties layer their own lost and found ordinances on top of that framework. Departments in places like West St. Paul, Minnetonka, and Isanti hold found property for at least 90 days unless someone claims it with satisfactory proof of ownership, and county sheriff's offices such as Anoka County publish retention schedules that stretch to six months for valuables. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Sheriff seizure of abandoned property (Sec. 345.15)
law.body: Under Minnesota Statutes 345.15, a county sheriff may seize and retain personal property abandoned on a public way, sidewalk, or other public premises. The sheriff must hold the property for at least three months before selling it at public auction, and reasonable public notice of the sale has to be given first.

law.title: Owner's 90 day reclaim window (Sec. 345.16)
law.body: Minnesota Statutes 345.16 gives the rightful owner 90 days from notice to reclaim seized or abandoned property, as long as they pay any expenses the agency incurred processing and storing it. Miss that window and the property can move to sale or disposal.

law.title: Local police lost and found ordinances
law.body: Most Minnesota police departments run their own lost and found program layered on top of state law. Ordinances in cities such as West St. Paul, Minnetonka, and Isanti require the chief of police to keep found property in a safe place for a period of at least 90 days, and it only goes back to the finder or gets released to a new owner if the true owner does not step forward with satisfactory proof.

law.title: Theft of lost or mislaid property (Sec. 609.52)
law.body: Minnesota's theft statute, Sec. 609.52, applies to someone who keeps property they know is lost or mislaid instead of turning it in. Penalties scale with value, misdemeanor theft covers property worth less than $500, and the statute lays out higher felony tiers as the dollar amount climbs.

law.title: County retention schedules vary
law.body: Retention periods are not identical everywhere. Anoka County's lost and found policy, for example, holds valuable and crucial items for six months, longer than the 90 day minimum set by many city ordinances, so how long your item sits in a property room depends on which department has it.

MN.whereTitle: Where items end up in Minnesota
MN.whereBody: A phone left at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) routes through airport lost and found, not the city police property room. A bag left on a Metro Transit bus or light rail line goes through Metro Transit's own lost and found, separate from Minneapolis or St. Paul police. Items left at Mall of America, US Bank Stadium, Target Center, or Xcel Energy Center typically go to venue or private security lost and found before anything reaches a municipal department, and county sheriff's offices handle property recovered from public ways and county parks under Sec. 345.15. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Departments in Minnesota generally require satisfactory proof of ownership before releasing found property, so be ready to describe a serial number, a passcode, a photo stored on the device, or some other private detail only the real owner would know.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Minnesota?
faq.a: No. Offering a reward is always your choice in Minnesota, not a legal requirement. Some finders and departments appreciate a token of thanks, but nothing in state law or local ordinance forces you to pay one to get your property back.

faq.q: How long will my local police department hold my item?
faq.a: It depends on the department. Many Minnesota cities hold found property for at least 90 days under local ordinance, while some counties, like Anoka County, extend that to six months for valuables. Statewide, Sec. 345.16 gives you 90 days from notice to reclaim seized property before it can be sold.

faq.q: What happens if nobody claims my lost item?
faq.a: Under Sec. 345.15, a sheriff who has held abandoned property for at least three months can sell it at public auction after giving reasonable public notice. Local police departments generally follow a similar path, holding property for their required period and then disposing of it or turning proceeds over to the city or county.

faq.q: Can I be in trouble for keeping something I found?
faq.a: Yes, potentially. Minnesota's theft statute, Sec. 609.52, covers keeping lost or mislaid property you know is not yours, with penalties that scale by value starting at misdemeanor theft for items worth less than $500. Turning found items in to police or the property's owner is the safer route.

intro: Mississippi does not run its lost and found rules through one single statute the way some states do. Instead, the state splits the job in two. Miss. Code § 21-39-21 gives municipalities the authority to take in, hold and eventually dispose of lost, stolen, abandoned or misplaced personal property that turns up in their jurisdiction, which is why what happens to a wallet handed to Jackson PD can look different from what happens in Gulfport or Southaven. Separately, Mississippi's Unclaimed Property Act, under Title 89, Chapter 12, forces banks, businesses and other holders to report money and intangible property to the State Treasurer once it has sat dormant for five years, with annual reports due before November 1.

For everyday items like phones, bags, jewelry or laptops, no state law fixes a mandatory holding period, so the clock and the claim process are set by whichever police department, airport, stadium or transit agency actually has your item. Mississippi's theft statutes do not spell out a separate crime for keeping something you found, so common law rules about lost, mislaid and abandoned property still shape whether holding onto someone else's item crosses into theft. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Disposition of Lost, Stolen, Abandoned or Misplaced Property (Miss. Code § 21-39-21)
law.body: This is the closest thing Mississippi has to a general lost and found statute. It authorizes municipal police departments to take custody of lost, stolen, abandoned or misplaced personal property, hold it, and eventually dispose of it if no owner comes forward. It does not set one statewide claim window, so the specifics are filled in city by city.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act, Title 89, Chapter 12, Five Year Dormancy
law.body: Banks, businesses and other holders of unclaimed funds or intangible property must report to the State Treasurer once property has been dormant for five years, with reports due before November 1 each year. Written notice is required at least 60 days before reporting for property valued over $50. This track exists for financial accounts and similar holdings, not for a phone or a suitcase someone turns in at a hotel front desk.

law.title: No Separate Crime for Keeping a Found Item
law.body: Mississippi's theft code, Title 97, does not carve out a distinct offense for finding something and simply keeping it. Common law distinctions between lost, mislaid and abandoned property still apply, and knowingly holding onto an item you know belongs to someone else can support a theft charge under general theft law depending on the facts.

law.title: Local Departments Set the Day to Day Rules
law.body: Because § 21-39-21 leaves the details to municipalities, police departments across Mississippi, from Jackson to Gulfport to Southaven, each set their own intake forms, holding periods and release procedures for lost property. There is no single statewide claim form or deadline that applies everywhere.

MS.whereTitle: Where items end up in Mississippi
MS.whereBody: Lost items in Mississippi tend to land wherever they were dropped. That means Jackson-Medgar Wiley Evers International Airport and Gulfport-Biloxi International Airport lost and found offices for anything left at security or on a flight, city transit systems like JATRAN in Jackson and the Coast Transit Authority on the Gulf Coast for anything left on a bus, and local police departments for items found on the street or in a park. Gulf Coast casinos, hotels, restaurants, and university venues around Ole Miss and Mississippi State each run their own internal lost and found desks. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: If it was turned in to a police department or a venue, you will usually need to prove ownership before they release it. That typically means describing the item accurately and giving one detail only the real owner would know, like a passcode, a serial number, or what is inside a bag, before staff hand it over.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Mississippi?
faq.a: No. Mississippi law does not require you to pay a reward for the return of a lost item. Offering one is always your choice, and many people find it speeds up how quickly someone bothers to turn something in.

faq.q: What happens if I turn something in to the police in Mississippi?
faq.a: Under Miss. Code § 21-39-21, municipal police departments can take custody of lost, stolen, abandoned or misplaced property, log it, and hold it while they try to locate the owner. If no one claims it, the department follows its own local disposal procedure, which varies by city.

faq.q: How long will Mississippi police hold my lost item before it is disposed of?
faq.a: There is no single statewide deadline. Mississippi law leaves the holding period up to each municipality's police department, so a phone held in Jackson may follow a different timeline than one held in Biloxi. The five year dormancy period under the Unclaimed Property Act applies to money and intangible holdings reported by businesses, not to a bag turned in at a police station.

faq.q: Does Mississippi have one statewide lost and found law?
faq.a: Not exactly. Miss. Code § 21-39-21 covers how municipalities handle lost, stolen, abandoned or misplaced personal property, while a separate Unclaimed Property Act under Title 89 handles dormant funds and intangible property held by banks and businesses. Everyday personal items fall back on common law and whatever policy the local department or venue has in place.

intro: Maine has an actual statute for this, which puts it ahead of many states. Title 25, Chapter 401 spells out what a finder and a law enforcement agency are supposed to do with lost, mislaid or stolen personal property, including a specific waiting period before anyone else can claim it. Maine also has a criminal statute that covers what happens when someone keeps property they know isn't theirs.
ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Property returned to finder (25 M.R.S. §3507)
law.body: Maine law lets any person who finds property surrender it to a law enforcement agency. That agency then becomes responsible for logging it and trying to locate the owner, which is why filing a report with the department nearest to where you lost something matters.

law.title: 30 day holding period (25 M.R.S. Chapter 401)
law.body: Once property is turned in, Maine's statute requires the owner or another person entitled to possession to be identified within a set window, at least 30 days from the initial date the property is logged, before the department can move toward disposing of it. This gives a real, if modest, window to file a report and get matched.

law.title: Custody and return duties (25 M.R.S. §3502)
law.body: Property believed to be abandoned, lost or stolen must be retained in custody by the chief of police or the law enforcement agency that received it. That custody requirement is the backbone of why calling or filing with the department directly is more useful in Maine than waiting and hoping.

law.title: Theft of lost, mislaid or mistakenly delivered property (17-A M.R.S. §356-A)
law.body: Maine's criminal code makes it a crime to knowingly keep lost, mislaid or mistakenly delivered property instead of trying to return it to its owner. The offense is treated more seriously when the property is worth more than $10,000 or when it is a firearm, which shows how much Maine law leans toward returning property rather than letting a finder keep it.

law.title: Statewide unclaimed property program
law.body: Maine's Unclaimed Property program, run out of the Treasurer's Office, handles unclaimed financial accounts and similar assets separately from personal items found in public. It is a useful backstop for things like old accounts, but it is not where your lost phone or wallet will show up. Local police property rooms are.

ME.whereTitle: Where items end up in Maine
ME.whereBody: Lost items in Maine tend to surface at Portland International Jetport, Bangor International Airport, on Greater Portland METRO buses, at ferry terminals serving the islands, at L.L. Bean and other retail anchors, at Acadia National Park and other state park sites, and at hotels, restaurants and event venues across Portland, Bangor, Augusta and the coastal tourist towns. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, once you can prove ownership. Departments in Maine typically ask for a description, and it helps to be ready with a private verification detail such as a serial number, an engraving, a saved photo, or the contents of a bag, something only the real owner would know.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Maine?
faq.a: No. Maine's statute doesn't require a reward for a finder or a police department to offer one. Offering a reward is always your choice, and it can sometimes speed up a return, but it is never required by law.

faq.q: How long does a police department in Maine have to hold my item before it's considered unclaimed?
faq.a: Under Title 25, Chapter 401, at least 30 days from the initial date the property is logged before the department can treat it as unclaimed and move toward disposal. Practices on exactly how disposal happens can vary by department.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps my lost item instead of turning it in?
faq.a: Maine's theft statute, 17-A M.R.S. §356-A, makes it a crime to knowingly retain lost, mislaid or mistakenly delivered property instead of trying to return it. The offense is more serious when the value is over $10,000 or the item is a firearm.

faq.q: Should I go straight to the airport or transit agency instead of the police?
faq.a: Both are worth contacting. Airports, transit agencies and venues often keep their own lost and found logs before an item is ever surrendered to a law enforcement agency under §3507, so checking both routes gives you the best chance of a match.

intro: Michigan is one of the few states with a dedicated lost property law on the books. Under the Michigan Compiled Laws, Chapter 434, a person who finds lost property has a legal duty to report the finding or deliver the property to a law enforcement agency in the jurisdiction where it was found. That duty, spelled out in MCL 434.22, sets Michigan apart from states that rely only on common law or local policy, and it shapes how police departments, airports, and businesses across the state actually handle turned-in items.

Once property reaches a Michigan law enforcement agency, the clock starts running under specific statutory timelines, and property of major value or collectible currency triggers extra reporting steps within 48 hours. Airports, transit agencies, stadiums, and retailers layer their own lost and found procedures on top of this state framework, which means where your item was lost often determines which office and which deadline actually apply. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Michigan's Lost Property Statute (MCL 434.21 et seq.)
law.body: Michigan Compiled Laws Chapter 434 is a true lost and found statute, not just an unclaimed property or theft law. It governs how finders, police departments, and owners are supposed to handle lost property found anywhere in the state, from a wallet on a sidewalk to a bag left at a bus stop.

law.title: Duty to Report or Deliver (MCL 434.22)
law.body: Anyone who finds lost property in Michigan is required to report the find or deliver the property to a law enforcement agency in the jurisdiction where it was found. This is a legal obligation, not just good manners, which is why filing a police report in the right city matters even for everyday items.

law.title: Major Value Property Gets Extra Steps (MCL 434.23)
law.body: When the found property qualifies as being of major value or is collectible currency, the receiving law enforcement agency must complete additional reports within 48 hours of the finder's report or delivery. Owners of higher value property may also receive a formal notice letter giving them roughly 6 months from the date of that letter to claim the item before it is treated as abandoned.

law.title: 3-Month Holding Period (MCL 434.24)
law.body: For most found property, if the legal owner has not claimed it within 3 months of it being reported or delivered to police, the holding law enforcement agency is permitted to dispose of it in any manner it chooses. This 3-month window is the general statutory baseline, though major value property follows the longer notice process above.

law.title: Separate Track: Michigan Unclaimed Property (MCL 567.238)
law.body: Financial assets like uncashed checks, forgotten accounts, and business-held funds move through a different system entirely, the Michigan Department of Treasury's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act. Holders generally report property valued over $50 after a dormancy period, commonly three years, and Treasury holds it for owners to claim later. This track does not apply to physical lost items like phones, bags, or jewelry, which stay under Chapter 434 and local police custody.

MI.whereTitle: Where items end up in Michigan
MI.whereBody: Detroit Metropolitan Airport (DTW), Gerald R. Ford International Airport in Grand Rapids, Bishop International in Flint, and Cherry Capital Airport in Traverse City each run their own lost and found desks that work alongside airline and TSA procedures. Transit riders lose items with DDOT and SMART in metro Detroit, The Rapid in Grand Rapids, and Ann Arbor's TheRide, all of which log found property separately from city police departments. Sports and entertainment venues like Ford Field, Comerica Park, and Little Caesars Arena, plus casinos such as MGM Grand Detroit and MotorCity Casino, and university campuses including the University of Michigan and Michigan State, all maintain their own lost and found points on top of the local police department that has jurisdiction under MCL 434.22. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you will need to prove ownership before a Michigan police department, airport, or venue releases the item to you. That usually means matching a description to one private detail about the item, such as an engraving, a photo on the device, or a receipt, that only the true owner would know.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Michigan?
faq.a: No. Michigan's lost property statute does not require owners to pay a reward to whoever finds and reports their property. Offering one is always your choice, and many people do so as a thank you, but it is never a legal condition for getting your item back.

faq.q: What happens if someone finds my item but does not report it?
faq.a: Under MCL 434.22, the finder is legally required to report the find or turn the property over to local law enforcement. Knowingly keeping property that belongs to someone else instead of reporting it can expose the finder to consequences well beyond the lost and found process.

faq.q: How long do I have to claim my lost item in Michigan?
faq.a: For most found property held by a Michigan law enforcement agency, you generally have about 3 months from when it was reported or delivered before the agency can dispose of it. Property classified as major value follows a longer notice process, giving owners roughly 6 months from a formal letter before it is considered abandoned.

faq.q: Where should I file a report first if I lost something in Michigan?
faq.a: Start with the law enforcement agency in the jurisdiction where you lost the item, since that is the agency Michigan law designates to receive found property under MCL 434.22. If you lost it at an airport, transit stop, or venue, also file with that location's own lost and found desk, since many operate independently before anything is handed to police.

intro: Missouri is one of the few states that actually wrote a lost property statute into its books. RSMo 447.010 spells out a duty for anyone who finds lost money or goods, and Chapter 447 goes on to build an entire state system for property that never gets claimed, run by the Missouri State Treasurer's Unclaimed Property Division rather than left to city hall. That split matters: a phone left on a MetroLink train or a bag found at a Cardinals game is handled by a local police department or venue lost and found desk, while cash, safe deposit box contents, and similar financial property that sits unclaimed for years eventually escheats to the state and shows up in the ShowMeMoney.com database.

On top of the finder's duty statute, Missouri's stealing law, RSMo 570.030, makes it a crime to knowingly keep property you know or should know is lost or mislaid, with penalties that scale by value, so 'finders keepers' is not actually the law here. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Duty of Finders (RSMo 447.010)
law.body: Missouri law directly addresses what a finder of lost money or goods is supposed to do, unlike states that rely purely on common law. This statute is the backbone of how local departments and courts in Missouri treat a found item and who is entitled to it if the owner never comes forward.

law.title: Stealing Statute (RSMo 570.030)
law.body: Knowingly keeping property you know or learn was lost or mislaid can be charged as stealing under RSMo 570.030. Penalties scale with value, from misdemeanor level for lower value items up to a Class C felony for property worth $25,000 or more, so returning a found item is not just courtesy, it avoids real criminal exposure.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Program (RSMo Chapter 447)
law.body: Financial property such as uncashed checks or safe deposit contents that goes unclaimed for a period generally described as three to five years, depending on the property type, is turned over to the Missouri State Treasurer. There is no time limit for the original owner or heir to file a claim, and the office even pays interest on cash property held for up to seven years.

law.title: Claim Windows and Disposal (15 CSR 50-3.090)
law.body: State regulations set concrete windows for acting on a claim: if proof of ownership is not presented promptly, property may be disposed of within one year, and a claimant is generally given thirty days to file paperwork once a claim process starts. Missing these windows can mean the difference between getting an item back and losing it to disposal.

law.title: Lost Versus Mislaid Property
law.body: Missouri courts distinguish between property that is truly lost and property that is merely mislaid, meaning intentionally set down and forgotten. Under this line of cases, the owner of the premises where an item was mislaid, not a random finder, is often the one entitled to hold it for the true owner, which affects where you should actually look first.

MO.whereTitle: Where items end up in Missouri
MO.whereBody: Missouri's two major air hubs, Kansas City International (MCI) and St. Louis Lambert International (STL), each run their own lost and found operations, as do regional transit systems like the Kansas City Area Transportation Authority (KCATA), the KC Streetcar, and St. Louis's Metro Transit under Bi-State Development. Sports and event venues add another layer entirely, from Arrowhead Stadium and Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City to Busch Stadium and the Enterprise Center in St. Louis, plus hotels, rideshare drivers, and restaurants across both metro areas and smaller cities like Springfield and Columbia. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove ownership. Departments and venues in Missouri typically ask for a private detail only the real owner would know, like a serial number, a specific photo on the phone, or what is inside a wallet, before releasing the item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Missouri?
faq.a: No. Nothing in Missouri's finder statute or its theft law requires a reward. Offering one is always your choice, and plenty of items are returned in Missouri with nothing more than a thank you.

faq.q: What happens to my lost item if no one claims it in Missouri?
faq.a: For physical items, local departments and venues generally hold property for a set period before disposing of it or donating it. For money and financial property specifically, Missouri law sends it to the State Treasurer's Unclaimed Property Division after a dormancy period of roughly three to five years, where it can be searched and claimed with no time limit.

faq.q: Can someone get in trouble for keeping something I lost?
faq.a: Yes. Under RSMo 570.030, knowingly keeping property you know or learn is lost or mislaid can be charged as stealing, with penalties that increase based on the value of the item, up to a Class C felony for property worth $25,000 or more.

faq.q: Do I have to file with police before checking an airport or transit lost and found?
faq.a: No, you can do both at the same time. Airports like MCI and STL, transit agencies like KCATA and Metro, and local police departments each keep separate lost and found records in Missouri, so filing everywhere at once gives your item the best chance of turning up.

intro: Nebraska is one of the few states where keeping something you find is spelled out as a crime in the criminal code itself. Neb. Rev. Stat. section 28-514 makes it theft to take control of property you know is lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake and then fail to take reasonable steps to return it to its owner. That single sentence shapes almost everything else in the state: if a stranger hands your dropped wallet to a store clerk or a police officer, the law expects that item to move toward you, not into someone else's pocket.

On the government side, when property ends up in the hands of a county sheriff, sections 69-1330 and 69-1331 set the clock: if it sits unclaimed for at least one hundred eighty days, the sheriff can sell it. Separately, Nebraska's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act runs on a much longer five year dormancy period, but that track is built for cash, checks, and business-held funds sitting at the State Treasurer's unclaimed property division, not for the phone you left in a booth at a Lincoln diner. City police departments, airports, and transit agencies layer their own retention windows on top of these statutes. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Theft of lost or mislaid property (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-514)
law.body: Nebraska criminal law directly addresses your situation. Anyone who comes into control of lost, mislaid, or misdelivered property and knows who it likely belongs to, but fails to take reasonable measures to return it, can be charged with theft. This gives you real leverage: a finder who ignores your identifying tags, receipts, or engraved initials is not just being unhelpful, they may be breaking the law.

law.title: County sheriff custody and sale (§§ 69-1330, 69-1331)
law.body: Property that comes into a county sheriff's possession is held for at least one hundred eighty days. If no owner claims it within that window, the sheriff may sell it. This is the practical deadline that matters most if your item was turned in to a sheriff's office rather than a city police department.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 69-1310 and related sections)
law.body: Cash, checks, and other property held by businesses and institutions follows a different, longer track. Nebraska's general dormancy period is five years before a holder must report the property to the State Treasurer's unclaimed property division, with shorter periods for things like wages and security deposits. This system exists for financial accounts, not for the backpack you left on a bus, but it explains why a bank or employer may hold funds far longer than a police department holds a physical item.

law.title: Local department policies fill the gaps
law.body: There is no single statewide statute telling every Nebraska police department exactly how long to hold a found wallet, phone, or bag before disposing of it, or how to log it. Cities such as Omaha and Lincoln, along with university police, transit agencies, and airport operators, each set their own intake, storage, and disposal timelines within the boundaries set by state theft and sheriff statutes.

NE.whereTitle: Where items end up in Nebraska
NE.whereBody: In Omaha, lost items most often surface at Eppley Airfield, with Metro transit buses and streetcars, at the CHI Health Center, or in the Old Market and stadium district around Nebraska football game days. In Lincoln, Lincoln Airport, StarTran buses, Memorial Stadium during Cornhuskers games, and the University of Nebraska-Lincoln campus police are common holding points. Statewide, county sheriff's offices, city police departments, hotels, and retail chains each keep their own found property logs. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you will need to prove ownership. Departments in Nebraska typically ask for a description that matches an internal detail they will not read aloud, such as a lock screen photo, a case contents list, or a serial number, along with the date and location you lost it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Nebraska?
faq.a: No. Nebraska law does not require you to pay a reward to get your property back. Offering one is always your choice, and it can sometimes speed up a return, but it is never a legal condition for reclaiming an item.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps my lost item instead of turning it in?
faq.a: Under Neb. Rev. Stat. section 28-514, a person who knowingly keeps lost or mislaid property without making a reasonable effort to return it to its owner can be charged with theft. This is one of the more direct legal protections a Nebraska resident has when trying to recover a specific dropped item.

faq.q: How long will a Nebraska sheriff's office or police department hold my item before disposing of it?
faq.a: If your item ends up with a county sheriff, sections 69-1330 and 69-1331 set a minimum one hundred eighty day holding period before it can be sold. City police departments, airports, and transit agencies set their own shorter or longer internal retention windows for lost property, so timing varies by exactly where you lost it.

faq.q: Does Nebraska have one statewide lost and found law like some other states?
faq.a: Not a single dedicated statute. Instead, Nebraska combines a criminal theft provision for lost or mislaid property, sheriff custody and sale rules, and a separate Unclaimed Property Act for cash and business-held funds. Local police departments and venues then apply their own procedures on top of that framework.

intro: Nevada does not have a single statewide statute that tells a stranger what to do the moment they pick up your phone or wallet. Instead, Nevada relies on its theft statute to create the incentive, NRS 205.0832(d) makes it a crime to keep lost, mislaid or misdelivered property when the circumstances give the finder a way to figure out who the true owner is. On top of that criminal backstop, individual cities and counties, along with the airports, casinos and transit agencies that see the heaviest foot traffic on the Strip and around Reno, run their own lost and found desks under local policy rather than one uniform state code.

There is a separate track for property that sits unclaimed inside a business or institution, bank accounts, safe deposit boxes, uncashed checks. That falls under NRS Chapter 120A, the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, administered by the Nevada Unclaimed Property program, and it works on a multi year abandonment clock that is very different from a wallet dropped on a casino floor. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Theft of Lost Property, NRS 205.0832(d)
law.body: Nevada's theft statute covers more than shoplifting. Under NRS 205.0832(d), a person commits theft if they come into control of lost, mislaid or misdelivered property under circumstances that give them a means of inquiry as to the true owner, and they keep it instead of trying to return it. Reported values matter for the charge, theft of property under $1,200 is a misdemeanor, and value between roughly $1,200 and $4,999 can be charged as grand larceny, a category D felony. This is the legal pressure that pushes most honest finders in Nevada to hand items to a business, venue or police department rather than keep them.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act, NRS Chapter 120A
law.body: Property that goes unclaimed inside a business, bank, or other holder, rather than being physically found by a person, is governed by the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act. Under this chapter property is generally presumed abandoned after 3 years with no owner activity, and holders must send written notice to the apparent owner before that presumption applies. The state's unclaimed property program, run through the Nevada Treasurer's office, is the right place to search if what you lost was money or a financial asset rather than a physical item someone might have picked up.

law.title: Local department and municipal ordinances
law.body: Because Nevada has no single statewide lost and found statute for finders on the street, cities fill the gap with their own rules. Elko's municipal code, for example, spells out the duty of city officers and employees who find lost money or property in a public place. Las Vegas Metropolitan Police, Reno Police, Henderson Police and the airport and transit authorities across the state each run their own intake procedures, holding periods, and claim verification steps, which is why the exact process for getting an item back depends heavily on which department or venue is holding it.

law.title: No uniform statewide holding period
law.body: Nevada law does not set one holding period that applies to every found item. Under NRS 120A property held by businesses is presumed abandoned after 3 years, but a phone or bag turned in at a casino, airport terminal, or police substation is governed by that specific department's own retention policy, which can run anywhere from a matter of weeks to several months before the item is logged as unclaimed and disposed of or auctioned.

NV.whereTitle: Where items end up in Nevada
NV.whereBody: In the Las Vegas area, lost items commonly surface at Harry Reid International Airport, at one of the Strip's casino resorts and their security or valet desks, or with the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the RTC transit system. In the north, Reno-Tahoe International Airport, RTC Washoe transit, and Reno or Sparks police departments handle their own found property. Smaller cities and counties, from Henderson to Elko, run their own municipal lost and found desks under local ordinance. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Is there a Nevada law that requires someone to turn in something they find?
faq.a: There is no single statewide statute that forces a finder to hand an item to police the moment they pick it up. Instead, Nevada's theft statute, NRS 205.0832(d), makes it a crime to keep lost, mislaid or misdelivered property when there is a reasonable way to identify the true owner, which is what pushes most finders to turn items in to a venue, transit agency or police department.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Most departments and venues in Nevada ask you to describe the item and provide at least one private detail that was not visible to whoever found it, such as a lock screen photo, a specific serial number, or what is inside a bag, before they release it to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Nevada?
faq.a: No. Nevada does not require a reward for the return of lost property. Offering one is always your choice, not a legal obligation, and plenty of items are returned with no reward at all.

faq.q: How long will a Nevada department or venue hold my item before disposing of it?
faq.a: It depends on who is holding it. There is no single statewide holding period for street level finds, each city, airport, casino, or transit agency sets its own retention window under local policy. Property held by businesses under the state's unclaimed property law is presumed abandoned after 3 years, but that applies to financial assets, not a phone or backpack sitting in a police property room.

faq.q: Does it matter how much my lost item is worth?
faq.a: It can matter if someone is caught keeping it rather than returning it. Nevada's theft of lost property statute treats value under $1,200 as a misdemeanor, and value between about $1,200 and $4,999 can be charged as grand larceny, a category D felony, which is one more reason most people who find something valuable in Nevada choose to turn it in.

intro: New Hampshire is one of the few states with a lost property statute that actually spells out numbers. RSA 471-C:13 tells police departments what to do with lost or abandoned personal property that comes through their doors, sets a dollar line at $250, and gives a 180 day holding period for higher value items before a department can dispose of them. The same chapter reaches into airport property rooms, and a separate criminal statute, RSA 637:6, makes it a theft offense to keep something you know was lost or mislaid instead of trying to return it. On top of that, the State Treasury runs a formal abandoned property program for financial assets like uncashed checks and forgotten accounts, which is a different track from a wallet or phone turned in at a police station.
ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Police Custody of Lost Property (RSA 471-C:13)
law.body: When someone turns lost or abandoned personal property into a New Hampshire police department, the statute sets the rules for what happens next. Property valued at $250 or more must be held for at least 180 days before the department can dispose of it, giving an owner a real window to claim it. Lower value items are handled on a faster timeline set by the individual department, so it pays to call the exact station that has your item as soon as you realize it is missing.

law.title: Theft of Lost or Mislaid Property (RSA 637:6)
law.body: New Hampshire criminal law does not treat a found wallet as finders keepers. Under RSA 637:6, a person who obtains property they know to be lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake commits theft if they do not make a reasonable, good faith attempt to return it to the owner. That legal duty is a big part of why calling local departments and businesses quickly, rather than assuming an item is gone for good, actually matters in this state.

law.title: Airport Lost and Found (RSA 471-C:13)
law.body: The same statute that governs municipal police departments extends to airport property rooms. An airport director or designee can dispose of noncontraband lost or abandoned property after it has sat unclaimed for 180 days, the same benchmark used elsewhere in the chapter. If you left something at a New Hampshire airport, that 180 day clock is your practical deadline to get a claim in.

law.title: State Treasury Abandoned Property Division (RSA 471-C:2)
law.body: Physical items and financial property follow different rules in New Hampshire. Intangible property such as uncashed checks, dormant accounts, and similar assets is presumed abandoned after five years and escheats to the state, managed through the Treasury's Abandoned Property Division at findnhmoney.gov. That system is separate from a police department's lost and found bin, so a missing phone and a forgotten account are not searched for in the same place.

NH.whereTitle: Where items end up in New Hampshire
NH.whereBody: A lost item in New Hampshire can land in several different systems depending on where it disappeared. Air travelers move through Manchester-Boston Regional Airport, Portsmouth International Airport at Pease, and often Boston Logan just across the border, each running its own lost and found under airport property room rules. Riders use the Manchester Transit Authority and COAST on the Seacoast, and venues from SNHU Arena to Bank of NH Pavilion, state parks, and college campuses like UNH and Dartmouth each keep their own lost and found with different holding periods. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you need to prove it is yours. New Hampshire police departments and venues typically ask for a description that includes a private detail, like a specific mark, contents, or serial number, that would not be visible from a photo alone. That step protects your property from being handed to the wrong person.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in New Hampshire?
faq.a: No. Nothing in New Hampshire law requires you to offer a reward for the return of lost property. It is always your choice, and plenty of items are returned with a simple thank you.

faq.q: How long will the police hold my item before it's disposed of or donated?
faq.a: Under RSA 471-C:13, items valued at $250 or more must be held for at least 180 days before a department can dispose of them. Items under that value are handled on a shorter, department set schedule, so confirm the exact timeline with the specific station holding your property.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps something they found instead of turning it in?
faq.a: New Hampshire treats that as theft. RSA 637:6 makes it a crime to knowingly keep property you know was lost or mislaid without making a reasonable effort to return it, which is part of why reporting to local police and nearby businesses is worth doing right away.

faq.q: What if my lost item was found at the airport?
faq.a: Airport property rooms in New Hampshire follow the same 180 day holding rule under RSA 471-C:13 as municipal police departments. Contact the specific airport's lost and found directly, since airlines and airport authorities often run separate intake systems for items found in terminals versus on aircraft.

intro: Montana does not run its found property system through a single lost-and-found statute the way some states do. Instead, the state relies on its criminal theft code to discourage people from pocketing what they find, and on a formal unclaimed property program at the Department of Revenue to take custody of items and money nobody claims. Local police departments, university police, and venues each set their own hold times and intake procedures on top of that framework.

If you lost something in Montana, the practical path usually runs through whichever police department, transit agency, or venue actually has it, followed by the state's Unclaimed Property Program if enough time passes with no owner found. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Theft of lost or mislaid property, MCA 45-6-302
law.body: Montana makes it a crime to keep lost or mislaid property instead of trying to return it to the owner or turning it in. A person convicted under this section can be fined up to $500 or jailed in the county jail for up to 6 months, so finders in Montana have a real legal reason to report what they pick up rather than keep it.

law.title: Report of abandoned property, MCA 70-9-808
law.body: When a holder has property valued at $50 or more that is presumed abandoned, Montana law requires written notice to the apparent owner sent not more than 120 days and not less than 60 days before the holder files a report with the state. This due diligence step is meant to catch owners before their property moves into the state's custody.

law.title: Montana Unclaimed Property Program
law.body: Property and money that goes unclaimed long enough is transferred to the Department of Revenue's Unclaimed Property Program, which holds it in safekeeping until the owner or an heir is located. You can search and file a claim directly through the state portal at revenue.mt.gov, or by calling the program.

law.title: Local department hold periods vary
law.body: Outside the state statutes, actual hold times depend on the department. Great Falls, for example, has an Evidence Technician follow up on claims within about 5 business days, while Montana State University police post found items and dispose of anything still unclaimed after 3 months. Always check with the specific department or venue holding your item.

law.title: Item-specific hold rules at institutions
law.body: Some Montana institutions set different hold windows by item type rather than a single statewide rule. Montana State University's lost and found policy, for instance, lists specific hold times such as 30 days for books before items are processed for disposal, so the clock can differ depending on what you lost and where.

MT.whereTitle: Where items end up in Montana
MT.whereBody: Lost items in Montana tend to land with whichever agency covers the spot where you lost them: airports like Bozeman Yellowstone International, Billings Logan International, Missoula International, Glacier Park International in Kalispell, and Helena Regional Airport all keep their own found property logs, as do transit systems like Mountain Line in Missoula, Streamline serving Bozoman and Big Sky, and MET Transit in Billings. Venues such as Yellowstone and Glacier National Park facilities, university campuses like the University of Montana and Montana State University, ski resorts including Big Sky and Whitefish Mountain Resort, and local police property rooms each run their own intake and hold periods. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: What should I do if I find lost property in Montana?
faq.a: Montana law does not let you simply keep something you find. Under MCA 45-6-302, holding onto lost or mislaid property instead of trying to return it or turning it in to police can be charged as theft, punishable by a fine up to $500 or up to 6 months in county jail, so report it to the local police department or the venue where you found it.

faq.q: How long will a Montana police department hold my item before I can claim it?
faq.a: There is no single statewide hold period, it depends on the department. Great Falls police typically have an Evidence Technician follow up on a claim within about 5 business days, while campus police at Montana State hold found items and may dispose of them after roughly 3 months if nobody claims them. Always confirm the specific timeline with the department holding your property.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you need to prove it is yours. Departments generally ask for a description that includes at least one private detail not visible from the outside, such as a passcode, a case contents list, an engraving, or a specific serial number, before releasing the item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Montana?
faq.a: No. Montana law does not require finders or owners to pay a reward. Offering one is always your choice, and plenty of items are returned with nothing more than a thank you.

faq.q: What happens if my lost item is never claimed?
faq.a: If a holder cannot locate you and your property is valued at $50 or more, Montana law requires written notice before the item or money is reported and eventually transferred to the state's Unclaimed Property Program at the Department of Revenue. You can search for and claim property held there directly through revenue.mt.gov.

intro: New Jersey is one of the few states with a real, purpose built lost property statute. The Legislature passed a dedicated law, often cited as the Lost or Abandoned Property Act and codified at N.J.S.A. 46:30C, that spells out exactly what a finder must do, how long an owner has to come forward, and what happens if nobody claims the item. That structure changes how a search in Newark, Jersey City, or along the Shore actually works, because the clock and the paperwork are defined by statute rather than left entirely to each department's own policy.

On top of the finders statute, New Jersey backs it with a criminal law, N.J.S.A. 2C:20-6, that makes it theft to keep property you know was lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake once you know or can reasonably find out who owns it. Municipal police departments layer their own procedures on top under N.J.S.A. 40A:14-157, covering how unclaimed money and property move through a station before a public auction. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Reasonable efforts to return it, N.J.S.A. 46:30C-4
law.body: New Jersey's finders law says a person may only claim lost property after making reasonable efforts to locate and notify the owner. Simply picking something up and holding onto it does not create any right to keep it, the statute requires an actual attempt to get it back to whoever lost it.

law.title: The 120 day window
law.body: Under New Jersey's lost or abandoned property act, if the owner does not reclaim an item within 120 days of the finder starting those reasonable efforts, the property can pass to the finder. That 120 day mark is the practical deadline that matters most for anyone trying to get an item back before someone else gains a legal claim to it.

law.title: Municipal police holding property, N.J.S.A. 40A:14-157
law.body: When a New Jersey police department takes in unclaimed money, it must turn it over to the municipal treasurer within 48 hours. Unclaimed property generally cannot be disposed of or auctioned for six months, and motor vehicles are held for that same six month period before the town can move on them.

law.title: Theft of lost or mislaid property, N.J.S.A. 2C:20-6
law.body: New Jersey treats keeping someone else's lost or mislaid property as a form of theft once the finder knows, or reasonably could learn, who the owner is. This is the criminal backstop that gives the civil finders rules teeth, and it is why departments and honest finders take turning items in seriously.

NJ.whereTitle: Where items end up in New Jersey
NJ.whereBody: Lost items in New Jersey tend to funnel through a handful of predictable systems. Newark Liberty International Airport and Atlantic City International Airport each run their own lost and found operations, separate from the airlines and from TSA checkpoints. NJ Transit, which covers commuter rail, light rail, and buses statewide, and PATH, which connects Jersey City, Hoboken, Newark, and Manhattan, each log found items by line and station. Large venues like MetLife Stadium, Prudential Center, and the boardwalks and beaches of the Jersey Shore have their own lost and found desks, and every municipal police department follows the state's 48 hour and six month holding rules under N.J.S.A. 40A:14-157 for anything turned in locally. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. New Jersey's finders statute puts the responsibility on the finder to try to return property to its rightful owner, and departments will typically ask you to describe a specific detail, like a case, an engraving, or a photo timestamp, that only the real owner would know before releasing it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. New Jersey law does not require owners to pay a reward to get lost property back. Offering one is always your choice, and while it can sometimes speed up a return, it has no bearing on your legal right to reclaim your own property.

faq.q: How long do I have to claim my lost item in New Jersey?
faq.a: The state's lost property act gives a finder 120 days from when they begin making reasonable efforts to locate you before the item can legally pass to the finder. Separately, many municipal police departments hold property for up to six months under N.J.S.A. 40A:14-157 before it goes to public auction, so acting quickly matters either way.

faq.q: What happens if nobody claims a found item in New Jersey?
faq.a: If the 120 day reasonable efforts period passes with no owner found, the finder can acquire the property under New Jersey's lost or abandoned property law. Items held by municipal police instead follow N.J.S.A. 40A:14-157, which keeps them for at least six months before the town can auction them off.

faq.q: Is it a crime to keep something you found in New Jersey?
faq.a: It can be. N.J.S.A. 2C:20-6 makes it theft to hold onto lost, mislaid, or mistakenly delivered property once you know, or could reasonably find out, who the owner is. Turning an item in to police or making a genuine attempt to return it is what keeps a finder on the right side of that law.

intro: New Mexico does not have one all purpose lost property law that tells every finder exactly what to do with a stray phone or wallet. Instead the state's rules are split across three places: a law enforcement statute that lets police take custody of unclaimed personal property, a criminal statute that specifically targets people who keep a lost credit card, and the Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, which governs abandoned money and financial assets through the Taxation and Revenue Department rather than physical items found on the street.

Because there is no single filing system for a lost backpack or set of keys, what happens to your item depends heavily on where you lost it and which department or business picked it up. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Held by Police (NM Stat. § 29-1-14)
law.body: When personal property with a fair market value greater than fifty dollars goes unclaimed by its true owner and is no longer needed as evidence, New Mexico law lets the holding law enforcement agency take custody of it and move toward disposition. This is the closest thing New Mexico has to a general found property statute, and it applies mainly to items that pass through a police department's property room.

law.title: Lost Credit Cards Are a Criminal Matter (NM Stat. § 30-16-27)
law.body: New Mexico specifically criminalizes possessing a credit card that was stolen, lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake. Holding onto someone else's card instead of turning it in or destroying it is a petty misdemeanor, which shows the state does expect finders to act in good faith even without a broad lost property code.

law.title: Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act (NMSA Chapter 7, Article 8A)
law.body: This act covers abandoned financial property such as uncashed checks, dormant accounts, and refunds, not physical items like phones or luggage. Holders must report property valued at fifty dollars or more to the Taxation and Revenue Department, which reviews claims within 90 days of filing plus an additional period before payment. It is searchable through the state's database and MissingMoney.com, but it will not help you locate a lost wallet.

law.title: General Theft Statute Fills the Gap
law.body: For everyday lost items that are not credit cards or financial property, New Mexico relies on its general theft statute. Petty theft involving property valued at $250 or less can carry fines up to $500 and up to six months in jail, which applies to someone who knowingly keeps a lost item rather than returning it.

law.title: Local Department and Venue Policies Govern the Rest
law.body: Because state law does not set a uniform turn-in procedure for phones, bags, or keys, what happens next depends on the police department, airport, transit agency, or business that recovers the item. Most keep found items for a set internal holding period before donating or disposing of them, so timing and the right point of contact matter.

NM.whereTitle: Where items end up in New Mexico
NM.whereBody: Lost items in New Mexico tend to land with whichever authority controls the location, since there is no statewide intake system. Albuquerque International Sunport and Santa Fe Municipal Airport each run their own lost and found desks, as do transit systems like ABQ RIDE and Rio Metro Regional Transit District. Venues such as Isotopes Park, Sandia Casino, and University of New Mexico facilities typically hold items briefly before handing them to campus or local police, and city police departments across Albuquerque, Santa Fe, and Las Cruces maintain their own property rooms under the state's unclaimed property statute. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you will need to prove ownership. Departments typically ask for a description that includes one private detail, such as a lock screen photo, a specific mark, or the contents of a bag, before releasing the item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in New Mexico?
faq.a: No. New Mexico has no statute requiring a reward for returned property. Offering one is always your choice, and many people find items are returned without any reward at all.

faq.q: What happens if no one claims my lost item?
faq.a: If police are holding it under the unclaimed property statute, they can move toward disposition once it is no longer needed as evidence. If it was cash or a financial instrument reported to the state, it may eventually be processed as unclaimed property with the Taxation and Revenue Department instead.

faq.q: Can I be in legal trouble for keeping something I found?
faq.a: Potentially, yes. Knowingly keeping a lost credit card is a specific petty misdemeanor under New Mexico law, and keeping other lost property you know belongs to someone else can fall under the general theft statute depending on its value.

faq.q: How long do New Mexico police departments hold found property?
faq.a: There is no single statewide number. Chapter 29 allows disposition once property is unclaimed and no longer needed as evidence, but the practical holding period is set by each department's own policy, so it is worth confirming directly with the department involved.

NM.disclaimer: This page provides general information about New Mexico law as of publication and is not legal advice. Procedures vary by city and department; verify details with your local authorities.

intro: North Carolina actually writes found property procedure into its General Statutes, which puts it in a different position than states that rely only on local policy. Chapter 15, Article 2 tells a finder and a law enforcement agency what happens next: the property is logged, a notice is published, and the owner has a window to come forward before the item can be released or disposed of.

On top of that criminal procedure chapter, North Carolina also treats failing to look for an owner as a form of theft, and it runs a separate statewide system, the Unclaimed Property Act, for money and financial assets that sit dormant with banks, courts and other holders. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Found property held by law enforcement (G.S. 15-11, Chapter 15, Article 2)
law.body: When a North Carolina law enforcement agency takes possession of found property, the statute requires publication of a notice to the owner. If nobody comes forward within 30 days after that publication, the agency can move toward releasing or disposing of the item, so acting fast and filing a report matters.

law.title: 180 day hold on seized and found items (G.S. 15-12)
law.body: Sheriffs and police departments in North Carolina are generally required to hold most confiscated and found property for 180 days after it comes into their custody before they can sell it or otherwise dispose of it, giving an owner a real window to claim it.

law.title: Keeping lost property can be charged as larceny (G.S. 14-72)
law.body: North Carolina law treats someone who has a reasonable way to find the owner of lost property, but makes no attempt to do so, as potentially guilty of theft. Larceny of property worth more than $1,000 is a Class H felony, and lesser amounts are prosecuted as a Class 1 misdemeanor, which is part of why turning items in to police rather than keeping them matters here.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act for money and financial assets (Chapter 116B)
law.body: Separately from lost personal items, North Carolina runs a statewide unclaimed property system through the State Treasurer for things like uncashed checks, safe deposit box contents and court funds. Dormancy periods vary by property type, generally around one year for government holders and up to five years for other property, and unclaimed funds are searchable through NCCash.gov.

NC.whereTitle: Where items end up in North Carolina
NC.whereBody: Lost items in North Carolina move through a mix of city police departments, county sheriffs, transit systems and private venues, and each one follows its own intake process on top of the state framework above. Charlotte Douglas International Airport, Raleigh-Durham International Airport and Piedmont Triad International Airport all run their own lost and found desks, as do transit systems like the Charlotte Area Transit System (CATS), GoTriangle and GoRaleigh. Arenas and stadiums such as Spectrum Center, PNC Arena and Bank of America Stadium, along with university campuses, hotels and rideshare drivers, each hold onto found items under their own house policies before anything reaches a city or county department. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. North Carolina departments and venues typically ask for a description that includes a private detail, something not visible from the outside, like what is saved on the lock screen, a mark inside a bag, or a specific accessory packed with the item, before releasing it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in North Carolina?
faq.a: No. North Carolina law does not require a reward for the return of lost property. Offering one is always your choice, and plenty of items are returned without any reward at all.

faq.q: How long will a North Carolina police department hold my item?
faq.a: Under Chapter 15, Article 2, an agency generally has to publish notice of found property, and the owner then has 30 days from that publication to claim it. Separately, G.S. 15-12 requires most seized or found property to be held for 180 days after it is taken into custody before disposal, so North Carolina gives owners more time than many states that have no statute at all.

faq.q: What if someone finds my item and just keeps it?
faq.a: North Carolina treats that as a potential crime. If a finder has a reasonable way to identify and locate the owner but makes no attempt to do so, that can be charged as larceny under G.S. 14-72, a felony above $1,000 in value and a misdemeanor below it. That legal backdrop is one reason it is worth filing a report and following up with police directly.

faq.q: Should I check NCCash.com for a lost item?
faq.a: NCCash.com is North Carolina's unclaimed property database, but it covers money and financial assets like uncashed checks, refunds and safe deposit box contents under Chapter 116B, not physical lost items like phones, bags or jewelry. For a physical item, your report needs to go to the local police department, transit agency or venue where it was lost, which is exactly what ReportLost handles.
