intro: North Dakota is unusual among the states ReportLost covers because it actually has a dedicated lost property statute on the books. North Dakota Century Code Chapter 60-01 spells out what happens when someone finds property that belongs to another person, including a specific rule about how long a law enforcement agency must hold it before the finder's claim is settled.

North Dakota also treats keeping someone else's lost property as a crime in its own right, not just a civil matter, under the state's theft code. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Lost Property Deposits (N.D.C.C. 60-01-41)
law.body: North Dakota's lost property chapter sets out what happens when found property or money is placed in the custody of a law enforcement agency. If the owner does not claim it within two years, the finder's claim against the original owner is exonerated by that surrender, meaning the two year window is the benchmark departments in North Dakota generally work from.

law.title: Theft of Lost or Mislaid Property (N.D.C.C. 12.1-23-04)
law.body: North Dakota makes it a crime to retain or dispose of property that you know has been lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, once you know or learn who the owner is or how to find them. This is the same theft statute used for shoplifting and other property crimes, so keeping a lost phone, wallet, or bag instead of turning it in can be charged as theft, a felony if the value tops $1,000 and a lesser offense below that.

law.title: Unclaimed Property and Escheatment (Title 47, Chapters 47-30.1 and 47-30.2)
law.body: Separate from a finder picking something up off the street, North Dakota law also covers property that banks, employers, and other businesses are holding for someone who never came back for it. Most property types are presumed abandoned after two or three years, safe deposit box contents after three years, and holders must report it to the North Dakota Unclaimed Property Division, which sends notices for amounts of $25 or more before turning funds over to the state.

law.title: Why the timeline matters
law.body: Because North Dakota actually names a two year holding period in Chapter 60-01, and a separate two to three year dormancy period for money held by businesses under Title 47-30.2, the practical answer to how long you have to claim something depends on whether a person or a department is holding it versus whether a bank or business is holding uncashed funds.

ND.whereTitle: Where items end up in North Dakota
ND.whereBody: Lost items in North Dakota tend to surface at Hector International Airport in Fargo, Bismarck Airport, and Grand Forks International Airport, along with transit systems like Fargo's MATBUS and Bis-Man Transit, university campuses such as NDSU and UND, and venues like the Fargodome, Bismarck Event Center, and the state's casinos and hotels. Local police departments also log found property under Chapter 60-01, and banks and employers escheat unclaimed funds to the state's Unclaimed Property Division. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. North Dakota departments typically ask for a description plus one detail only the true owner would know, such as a lock screen photo, a serial number, or what is inside a bag pocket, before releasing property.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in North Dakota?
faq.a: No. Offering a reward is always your choice under North Dakota law, not a legal requirement. Some finders appreciate one, but you are never obligated to offer money to get your own property back.

faq.q: How long will the police hold my item in North Dakota?
faq.a: Under N.D.C.C. 60-01-41, once found property or money is placed in a law enforcement agency's custody, the general benchmark is two years before an unclaimed item's status changes. Individual departments may have their own shorter storage practices, so check locally.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps my lost item instead of turning it in?
faq.a: North Dakota's theft statute, N.D.C.C. 12.1-23-04, makes it a crime to retain or dispose of property you know is lost or mislaid once you can identify the owner. Depending on the value, this can be charged as a felony or a misdemeanor.

faq.q: What about cash or property that ends up with a bank or business instead of a finder?
faq.a: That falls under North Dakota's separate unclaimed property law. Most property is presumed abandoned after two or three years of no owner contact, and the holder must report it to the North Dakota Unclaimed Property Division, which you can search directly if a bank or employer says they escheated your funds.

ND.disclaimer: This page provides general information about North Dakota law as of publication and is not legal advice. Procedures vary by city and department, verify details with your local authorities.

intro: Oklahoma treats a lost wallet, phone, or bag differently than most states because the state actually criminalizes keeping what you find. Under 21 O.S. §1702, a person who comes into possession of lost property and fails to make a reasonable effort to locate the owner can be charged with larceny of lost property, a misdemeanor if the item is worth less than $1,000 and a felony above that. That statute gives Oklahoma finders a real incentive to turn things in, and it gives you, the owner, a state law working in your favor the moment something goes missing.

Once an item is turned in, what happens next depends on which department has it. Local police property rooms, from Oklahoma City to Tulsa to smaller municipalities, operate under their own retention rules, and separate provisions in Title 22 and Title 60 govern how sheriffs, campus police, and the state Treasurer handle property nobody claims. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Larceny of Lost Property, 21 O.S. §1702
law.body: If someone finds your property and knows or can reasonably discover who owns it, but keeps it anyway without a reasonable attempt to return it, they can be prosecuted. Items under $1,000 in value make it a misdemeanor, and higher values can push the charge into felony territory with penalties reported as high as eight years. This statute is the backbone of Oklahoma's lost property law and it applies statewide, not just in one city.

law.title: Finder's Option to Retain or Relinquish, Title 11 §34-104G
law.body: Oklahoma statute requires officers who take in found property to give the finder a choice, either they can retain a future claim to the item if it goes unclaimed, or they relinquish that claim entirely. This affects how Tulsa and other departments log found items and matters if you are trying to identify who found your property and where it went.

law.title: Holding periods set locally, disposal under 22 O.S. §1325
law.body: There is no single statewide holding period for found property. Oklahoma City's Police Department Property Management Unit keeps unclaimed items a minimum of three months, and often longer. Other cities set their own windows under local ordinances, some as short as ten to thirty days, before property held by a sheriff's office or campus police agency can be sold, donated, or destroyed under 22 O.S. §1325.

law.title: Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, Title 60
law.body: Cash, checks, and other financial property that go unclaimed for a statutory period end up reported to the Oklahoma State Treasurer under the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act. There is no deadline to claim property once it lands in this system, and the Treasurer maintains a free searchable database at yourmoney.ok.gov. This track is separate from physical lost items handled by police property rooms.

OK.whereTitle: Where items end up in Oklahoma
OK.whereBody: Lost items in Oklahoma tend to surface through a handful of predictable channels. Will Rogers World Airport in Oklahoma City and Tulsa International Airport both run their own lost and found desks for anything left at security, gates, or baggage claim. EMBARK in Oklahoma City and Tulsa Transit handle items left on buses and at stops, and city police property rooms, from OKC to Tulsa to Norman, are the default destination for anything turned in from a sidewalk, park, or store. Add in the usual venues, arenas, hotels, and college campuses with their own campus police, and the number of possible drop off points adds up fast. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you need to prove ownership first. Departments typically ask for a description that includes something only the real owner would know, like a serial number, a specific mark, or the contents of a bag. Once you clear that step, the property room releases the item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Oklahoma?
faq.a: No. Oklahoma law does not require owners to pay a reward for the return of lost property. Offering one is always your choice, and plenty of items are returned with nothing more than a thank you.

faq.q: What happens if someone keeps what they find instead of reporting it?
faq.a: They can be charged under 21 O.S. §1702, larceny of lost property. Value determines severity, under $1,000 is a misdemeanor, and higher amounts can be charged as a felony. Knowing this statute exists is useful leverage if you can identify who found your property.

faq.q: How long will the police hold my item before disposing of it?
faq.a: It depends on the department. Oklahoma City's Property Management Unit holds items a minimum of three months and often longer, while some smaller municipalities work on shorter windows, sometimes ten to thirty days, before selling or disposing of unclaimed property under state and local rules. Check with the specific department holding your item.

faq.q: What if my lost item was cash, a check, or another financial instrument?
faq.a: That falls under the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act rather than a police property room. Search the Oklahoma State Treasurer's free database at yourmoney.ok.gov, there is no deadline to claim property once it has been reported to the state.

OK.disclaimer: This page provides general information about Oklahoma law as of publication and is not legal advice. Procedures vary by city and department, verify details with your local authorities.

intro: Oregon is one of the few states with a detailed statute built specifically for lost property. ORS Chapter 98 spells out what a finder has to do, what happens to money or goods worth $250 or more, and how a police department or city eventually disposes of items nobody claims. That statute, plus a separate criminal law making it theft to keep something you know is lost or mislaid, shapes how lost and found actually works from Portland to Bend.

Because the state law sets a real duty to report a find and a real dollar threshold, Oregon lost and found is less about vague 'best practices' and more about following a specific process, then layering city and county policies on top of it for how long an item sits in a property room. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Finder's duty for items worth $250 or more (ORS 98.005)
law.body: If someone finds money or goods valued at $250 or more and the owner is unknown, Oregon law requires the finder to give notice within 10 days of finding it, and to publish notice once a week for two consecutive weeks. This is the backbone of Oregon lost and found law and is why many local police departments, from Beaverton to Lane County, walk finders through this exact notice process.

law.title: Theft of lost or mislaid property (ORS 164.065)
law.body: Oregon treats keeping someone else's lost or mislaid property as theft if you know, or have good reason to know, it belongs to another person and you fail to take reasonable steps to return it. This is a criminal statute, not just a moral rule, which is part of why turning found items in to police or a venue is the expected practice statewide.

law.title: Disposition of unclaimed property (ORS 98.245)
law.body: Once property found, seized, or held by a city or county goes unclaimed, ORS 98.245 governs how that agency can dispose of it, whether that means auctioning it, donating it, or otherwise closing out the file. Several Oregon cities reference this section directly in their own municipal codes for police property rooms.

law.title: Local holding periods before disposal
law.body: Individual departments set their own timelines within the state framework. Some cities hold unclaimed property for 90 days after it is turned in, others count 60 days following the conclusion of any related criminal case, and still others require a claim within 30 days after a notice is sent. There is no single statewide number, so the clock that matters is the one set by the department actually holding your item.

law.title: Where to start a claim
law.body: Because Oregon does not run lost and found through a single statewide portal, the practical starting point is always the specific city police department, county sheriff's office, or transit and venue lost and found line that would plausibly have picked up the item, which is why local contacts matter more than a general state number.

OR.whereTitle: Where items end up in Oregon
OR.whereBody: In Portland, items go through Portland Police Bureau property units, TriMet lost and found for buses, MAX light rail and the streetcar, and Portland International Airport (PDX) lost and found. In Eugene, Lane County Sheriff's Office and Eugene Police Department handle turned in property, alongside Eugene Airport (EUG) and Lane Transit District. Salem, Bend, and other cities route items through their own police departments and city hall, plus airport counters at Eugene or Portland if travel was involved, and countless items surface at malls, stadiums, hotels, and rideshare dropoffs across the state. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: You have to show it is actually yours. Departments generally ask for a description that includes at least one private detail, like a specific mark, a passcode, or contents inside a bag, that would not be obvious to someone who only saw the item from the outside.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Oregon?
faq.a: No. Oregon's finder statute focuses on notice and claim procedures, not on requiring a reward. Offering one is always your choice, not a legal obligation.

faq.q: What happens if I find something worth $250 or more in Oregon?
faq.a: Under ORS 98.005, you are required to give notice within 10 days of finding it and to publish notice once a week for two consecutive weeks if the owner is unknown. Many people simply hand the item to local police, who can walk you through this process.

faq.q: How long will a police department in Oregon hold my lost item?
faq.a: It depends on the department. Some cities hold property for 90 days, others count 60 days after any related criminal case ends, and some require a claim within 30 days of a notice being sent. Always confirm the specific holding period with the department that has your item.

faq.q: Can I get in trouble for keeping something I found in Oregon?
faq.a: Yes. ORS 164.065 makes it theft to keep property you know or have good reason to know is lost or mislaid, without taking reasonable steps to return it. This is why prompt reporting matters, both for the owner's sake and the finder's.

intro: In Rhode Island, what happens to something you lose depends on which door it walks through. Hand a wallet to a beat cop in Providence and it lands under Rhode Island General Laws Title 6, Chapter 53, which sets a fourteen day holding period starting the moment the police chief's office logs the report. Turn in money or goods and a separate statute, Title 33, Chapter 21.2, gives the finder a six month window to establish a claim before the property can be treated as abandoned. Airports, colleges, and transit agencies layer their own written policies on top of that, often with their own value thresholds and hold times, so the same lost backpack can be governed by two or three different rules depending on where it surfaces.
ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Fourteen day police holding period (R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-53-5)
law.body: Once a police chief's office receives and logs a report of found property, the fourteen day holding clock starts running from that delivery date, not from when the item was actually found. This is the window during which an owner should come forward at the department that logged the report.

law.title: Finder's claim window (R.I. Gen. Laws § 33-21.2-4)
law.body: When money or goods are delivered to police, the person who found them has up to six months from the date of that report and delivery to file a claim. If nobody, including the finder, claims the property within six months, it can be disposed of under the statute.

law.title: Larceny and mislaid property (R.I. Gen. Laws Title 11, Chapter 41 and § 11-49-3)
law.body: Rhode Island's larceny statute covers property taken or kept without the owner's consent, with penalties scaled to value, for example theft of $1,500 or less can carry up to one year imprisonment and a fine up to $500. A separate provision, § 11-49-3, makes it a crime to knowingly keep or use a credit card you know was lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake, which is the state's clearest statement on knowingly holding onto someone else's mislaid item.

law.title: Local department and campus policies
law.body: Agencies fill in the gaps the state statutes leave open. Rhode Island College's lost and abandoned property policy, for example, holds items worth more than $100 for a full year from the date they are delivered to the department, well beyond the fourteen day or six month statutory windows, so always check the specific policy of the department or venue holding your item.

law.title: State Treasury unclaimed property (findrimoney.gov)
law.body: Cash equivalents, safe deposit contents, and other intangible unclaimed property valued at $50 or more eventually get reported to the Rhode Island Office of the General Treasurer and can be searched or claimed through findrimoney.gov, separate from the item recovery process handled by local police.

RI.whereTitle: Where items end up in Rhode Island
RI.whereBody: Lost items in Rhode Island tend to collect at a handful of predictable spots: T.F. Green International Airport in Warwick, RIPTA buses and the Providence intermodal transit hub, the MBTA commuter rail line running between Providence and Boston, college campuses like Brown, URI, and Rhode Island College, and venues such as the Dunkin' Donuts Center and Twin River Casino. Each keeps its own lost and found desk, on its own hold schedule, before an unclaimed item is turned over to city police or, for cash and valuables, the state Treasury. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, once you prove ownership. Departments typically ask you to describe the item and confirm one private detail that would not be obvious from looking at it, such as what is saved in a phone's lock screen or a specific mark inside a bag, before releasing it to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Rhode Island?
faq.a: No. Nothing in Rhode Island's found property or larceny statutes requires a reward. Offering one is always your choice, and finders are not entitled to demand payment before returning an item.

faq.q: How long will the police hold my lost item before it's considered abandoned?
faq.a: It depends on the track. Under R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-53-5, the police holding period is fourteen days from when the report was delivered to the chief's office. If money or goods were formally reported and delivered under § 33-21.2-4, the finder's claim window runs six months. Some venues, like college campuses, set their own longer holds, so always confirm with the specific department.

faq.q: What if the person who found my item just keeps it?
faq.a: Rhode Island's larceny law in Title 11, Chapter 41 applies to property kept without the owner's consent, and § 11-49-3 specifically criminalizes knowingly keeping a lost or mislaid credit card. If you can identify who has your property and they refuse to return it, file a police report describing the item and the circumstances.

faq.q: Where do I check for lost cash or valuables that were never claimed?
faq.a: If an item was cash, a check, or similar unclaimed property valued at $50 or more, it may eventually be reported to the Rhode Island Office of the General Treasurer. You can search or file a claim directly through findrimoney.gov.

intro: South Carolina is one of the few states that actually wrote a found property statute into its code instead of leaving the whole question to common law. Title 27, Chapter 21 tells a sheriff or police chief what to do once someone turns an item in, including a notice deadline and a claim window, so if you lost something in Charleston, Columbia, Greenville, or Myrtle Beach, there is an actual state law timeline running in the background, not just department habit.

South Carolina also runs a completely separate system, the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, for money and financial assets like dormant bank accounts or uncashed checks, which is a different track from the wallet you dropped at a stadium or the phone left in a rideshare. law.title: S.C. Code Title 27, Chapter 21, found property
law.body: South Carolina's found property statute requires a sheriff or chief of police who takes in found property to provide notice within fifteen days. This is a real, codified duty, not just internal department policy, which sets South Carolina apart from states that have no dedicated lost property statute at all.

law.title: The sixty day claim window
law.body: Under the same chapter, if the property is not reclaimed within sixty days of that mailed notice, its status changes under state law. That sixty day mark is the number to watch if you are trying to get an item back from a South Carolina police department, and it lines up with what departments actually apply on the ground.

law.title: How departments apply it, Columbia PD example
law.body: Columbia Police Department's own Evidence and Property Control policy states that found or recovered property that has not been claimed will be disposed of after sixty days at the discretion of the Evidence Supervisor, matching the state law timeline. Other departments across the state run their own evidence rooms the same way, so always confirm the specific hold period and required proof with the department that has your item.

law.title: Unclaimed Property Act, Title 27, Chapter 18, a different track
law.body: South Carolina's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, administered by the State Treasurer, deals with money and financial holdings, not the phone or bag you left somewhere. Property under that Act is presumed abandoned after a set number of years and can be sold at public sale within three years of the state receiving it under Section 27-18-230. If you lost a physical item, Chapter 21 and local police property rooms are the right place to look, not the Treasurer's unclaimed funds search.

SC.whereTitle: Where items end up in South Carolina
SC.whereBody: Lost items in South Carolina move through a mix of airports, transit systems, and tourist infrastructure. Charleston International Airport, Columbia Metropolitan Airport, Greenville-Spartanburg International Airport, and Myrtle Beach International Airport each run their own lost and found desks. Transit riders deal with CARTA in Charleston, the COMET in Columbia, and Greenlink in Greenville, all separate from city police property rooms. Add in the beaches of Myrtle Beach and Hilton Head, historic sites like Fort Sumter, hotels, stadiums, and rideshare vehicles, and an item can land in several different systems depending on exactly where it was dropped. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Departments in South Carolina typically ask for a description that includes at least one private detail, like a lock screen photo, a serial number, or what is inside a bag, before they release it to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in South Carolina?
faq.a: No. South Carolina law does not require a reward for returned property. Offering one is always your choice, and plenty of items get returned with a simple thank you.

faq.q: How long will a South Carolina police department hold my found item?
faq.a: Under Title 27, Chapter 21, a sheriff or chief of police must give notice within fifteen days of taking in found property, and if it is not reclaimed within sixty days of that notice its status changes under the statute. Local practice, like Columbia's evidence policy, follows that same sixty day mark, but always confirm directly with the department holding your item.

faq.q: What is the difference between lost and found property and South Carolina's Unclaimed Property Program?
faq.a: They are two different systems. Title 27, Chapter 21 and local police property rooms handle physical items like phones, bags, and jewelry. The Unclaimed Property Act, run by the State Treasurer, handles money and financial assets such as dormant bank accounts or uncashed checks. Searching the Treasurer's database will not help you find a lost phone or wallet.

faq.q: What should I do first if I lost something in South Carolina?
faq.a: File a report with the police department covering where you lost it, and separately contact the airport, transit agency, or venue involved, since each keeps its own found property log. ReportLost files with the right ones and keeps checking on your behalf.

intro: South Dakota is one of the few states with an actual lost and found statute on the books, not just borrowed theft law. SDCL Chapter 43-41, titled Lost and Found Property, spells out what a finder is supposed to do and puts the burden on the person claiming the item to prove it is actually theirs before it gets handed back.

That second part matters more in South Dakota than in most states. A finder who knowingly keeps something they know was lost, strayed, or mislaid can be charged under SDCL 22-30A-6, theft of lost or mislaid property, so the statute gives people a real incentive to turn things in rather than pocket them. From there, how long a department holds an item before it is released, donated, or disposed of is set locally, city by city, not by one statewide clock. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Lost and Found Property, SDCL Chapter 43-41
law.body: South Dakota's own lost property chapter sets the duty of a person who finds lost personal property and requires a claimant to prove ownership before the item is returned. It is a rare thing for a state to spell out this directly, and it is the backbone of how South Dakota handles turned-in property.

law.title: Theft of Lost or Mislaid Property, SDCL 22-30A-6
law.body: Anyone who comes into control of property they know to have been lost, strayed, or mislaid and keeps it instead of trying to return it can be charged with theft under this section. It applies whether the item was picked up on a sidewalk, left on a bar counter, or found in a parked car.

law.title: Local holding periods, city by city
law.body: South Dakota does not set one statewide hold time for turned-in property. Cities set their own rules through municipal ordinance. Tea, South Dakota, for example, allows its police department to dispose of abandoned property after it has been held 30 days unclaimed. Sioux Falls, Rapid City, and other departments run on their own internal schedules, so the real answer depends on which department has your item.

law.title: South Dakota Unclaimed Property Act, SDCL 43-41B
law.body: When lost value takes the form of dormant bank accounts, uncashed checks, or forgotten safe deposit box contents rather than a physical item handed to police, it falls under this chapter instead. Holders must mail notice for property worth fifty dollars or more, and the state treasurer's office holds the funds through cash.sd.gov until an owner or heir files a claim, with no deadline to come forward.

law.title: Value thresholds under South Dakota theft law
law.body: If a found item's value becomes a factor in a criminal case, South Dakota grades theft by dollar amount. Property worth 401 to 1,000 dollars is petty theft in the first degree, a class 1 misdemeanor, one more reason South Dakota law pushes finders toward turning items in rather than keeping them.

SD.whereTitle: Where items end up in South Dakota
SD.whereBody: Lost items in South Dakota tend to surface at a handful of predictable places. Sioux Falls Regional Airport, known locally as Joe Foss Field, and Rapid City Regional Airport both run their own lost and found desks separate from airline counters. Transit riders on Sioux Falls Transit should check with the agency directly, and anything left at Mount Rushmore, Crazy Horse Memorial, Badlands National Park, or the casinos and hotels around Deadwood usually goes to that specific site's office rather than city police. Arenas like the Denny Sanford Premier Center in Sioux Falls hold items from concerts and games separately too. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: South Dakota law puts the burden on you, the claimant, to prove ownership before an item is handed back under SDCL 43-41. Departments typically ask for a description that includes a detail only the true owner would know, like a case scratch, an inscription, or a saved photo on a phone, before releasing it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in South Dakota?
faq.a: No. South Dakota law does not require a reward for returned property. Offering one is always your choice, and plenty of items are turned in and returned with no reward at all.

faq.q: What happens if I keep something I found instead of turning it in?
faq.a: You can be charged under SDCL 22-30A-6, theft of lost or mislaid property, if you knew the item was lost, strayed, or mislaid and kept it anyway. The safer route, and the one the statute is built around, is reporting the find to police or making a real effort to locate the owner.

faq.q: How long will South Dakota police hold my lost item before it's disposed of?
faq.a: There is no single statewide number. Individual cities set their own holding periods by ordinance. Tea, South Dakota, for instance, can dispose of unclaimed abandoned property after 30 days. Larger departments in Sioux Falls or Rapid City may run different schedules, so it is worth asking the specific department holding your item.

faq.q: What if my lost item is actually a dormant account, uncashed check, or forgotten valuables in a safe deposit box?
faq.a: That falls under a different law, the South Dakota Unclaimed Property Act, SDCL 43-41B. Holders must mail notice once the value reaches fifty dollars, and the state treasurer's office keeps the funds available at cash.sd.gov with no deadline for the rightful owner or their heirs to claim them.

intro: Tennessee does not have one single statute that tells every finder exactly what to do with a lost wallet, phone, or bag, the way some states do. What governs a lost item in Memphis, Nashville, Knoxville, or Chattanooga is a mix of old common law duties, the state's general theft statute, and whatever policy the local police or sheriff's department has written down for its property room. Tennessee Code Section 8-8-501 gives county sheriffs authority to dispose of abandoned, stolen, or recovered property that nobody claims, and Section 39-14-103 makes knowingly keeping property that belongs to someone else a form of theft, but neither section spells out a statewide finder's process the way a dedicated lost property law would.

That gap gets filled at the city and county level. Knoxville Police, for example, publish a policy of holding found property for 90 days before the finder can even file a claim to keep it, and other Tennessee departments run their own timelines. Separately, the Tennessee Department of Treasury runs the Unclaimed Property Act for money, uncashed checks, and similar financial assets, which is a different track from a phone left in an Uber. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: No single statewide finder statute
law.body: Tennessee relies on common law duties and department policy rather than one dedicated lost property statute. A finder who discovers a wallet, bag, or device generally has an obligation to make a reasonable effort to return it or turn it in to local police, but the specific steps and deadlines are set by the city or county, not by a uniform state code section.

law.title: Theft of property, T.C.A. § 39-14-103
law.body: Tennessee's theft statute covers knowingly obtaining or exercising control over property that belongs to someone else with intent to deprive them of it. Courts and practitioners have applied this same theft framework to lost and mislaid property, so a finder who keeps something valuable instead of trying to return it or reporting it can face theft exposure, with classification tied to the value of the item.

law.title: Sheriff disposal authority, T.C.A. § 8-8-501
law.body: When recovered or abandoned property is not claimed, this section authorizes the county sheriff to dispose of it. Local police departments build their own hold periods around this authority, for example Knoxville's policy holds found items for 90 days and then gives the finder 10 days to file a claim before the property can be disposed of or released, unless the true owner claims it first.

law.title: Tennessee Unclaimed Property Act, T.C.A. §§ 66-29-101 to 155
law.body: This separate statute governs unclaimed money, uncashed checks, and similar intangible or financial property held by banks, employers, and other businesses, which gets reported to the state Treasury and searchable through ClaimItTN.gov. It is a different legal track from a lost phone or bag found in public, but Tennessee residents sometimes encounter both systems while searching for missing property.

TN.whereTitle: Where items end up in Tennessee
TN.whereBody: Lost items in Tennessee tend to funnel through a handful of predictable places. Nashville International Airport and Memphis International Airport both run their own lost and found desks, as do smaller commercial airports around the state. Local transit agencies like WeGo Public Transit in Nashville, Memphis Area Transit Authority, and Knoxville Area Transit hold items left on buses and trolleys. Large venues such as Bridgestone Arena, Nissan Stadium, the Grand Ole Opry, Broadway's honky tonk district, and Beale Street clubs collect items separately, and the Great Smoky Mountains region has its own park and visitor center lost and found points. City police property rooms in Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville, and Chattanooga are usually the final stop once a rideshare driver, a bar, or a stranger turns something in. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: You generally need to prove the item is yours before a Tennessee police property room or a business lost and found will release it. That usually means describing something specific that would not be obvious to a stranger, like a passcode, a case detail, or a private message saved on the device, along with matching identification.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Tennessee?
faq.a: No. Tennessee does not require owners to pay a reward to get lost property back. If you want to offer one to encourage a faster return, that is always your choice, never a legal obligation.

faq.q: What happens if nobody claims my lost item?
faq.a: Local policy controls this, not a single state deadline. Under Knoxville's published policy, for instance, found property is held 90 days and then the finder has 10 days to file a claim, after which the department can dispose of it under the sheriff's disposal authority in T.C.A. § 8-8-501. Other Tennessee cities set their own timelines.

faq.q: Can the person who found my item just keep it?
faq.a: Not safely. Tennessee's theft of property statute, T.C.A. § 39-14-103, has been applied to people who knowingly keep lost or mislaid property instead of trying to return it, and the classification of the offense depends on the item's value. Turning it in to local police is the finder's safest route.

faq.q: Is this the same as unclaimed money held by the state?
faq.a: No. Tennessee's Unclaimed Property Act, T.C.A. §§ 66-29-101 to 155, deals with things like uncashed checks and dormant accounts held by banks and businesses, searchable through the Treasury's ClaimItTN.gov. A lost wallet, phone, or bag found in public goes through local police property rooms instead, which is the track ReportLost focuses on.

intro: Utah is one of the few states with a real, dedicated lost and found statute. Title 77, Chapter 11D of the Utah Code, the Lost or Mislaid Property Act, spells out what a finder has to do, what a local law enforcement agency has to publish, and how long property has to sit before anyone can claim it or dispose of it. That is different from states that only rely on old common law rules, and it means a lost wallet, phone, or bag turned in to a Utah police department or sheriff's office follows a specific legal sequence rather than an informal one.

Utah also has a specific criminal statute for keeping something you know was lost or mislaid, so the law treats pocketing a found item as more than just bad manners. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Lost or Mislaid Property Act, Utah Code Title 77, Chapter 11D
law.body: Utah has a statewide statute covering property that comes into the possession of a peace officer or local law enforcement agency after being found. It sets out what happens from the moment property is turned in to the point it is either claimed, released to the finder, or disposed of.

law.title: Finder's statement, Utah Code 77-11d-103
law.body: A person who finds lost or mislaid property and delivers it to a local law enforcement agency must sign a statement on a form provided by that agency. This creates a paper trail tying the found item to the person who turned it in and the date it arrived.

law.title: Publication, posting and holding period, Utah Code 77-11d-105
law.body: The agency has to publish and post notice of the found property, and it cannot dispose of the item until at least eight days after that publication and posting. If no owner comes forward within nine days of publication, the agency notifies the finder, who may then have a claim to the property. Some campuses and departments hold items even longer, for example University of Utah surplus holds lost property for thirty to sixty days.

law.title: Theft of lost, mislaid, or mistakenly delivered property, Utah Code 76-6-407
law.body: Utah's theft code specifically covers keeping property you know was lost, mislaid, or delivered by mistake. Holding on to a found item without making a reasonable effort to return it or turn it in can be prosecuted as theft, separate from the civil process of claiming abandoned property.

law.title: City ordinances mirror the state process
law.body: Cities including Salt Lake City have their own municipal code sections on disposition of lost, mislaid and unclaimed property, generally following the same publication and minimum holding period set at the state level, with unclaimed items eventually released to the finder or the city.

UT.whereTitle: Where items end up in Utah
UT.whereBody: Lost items in Utah typically surface at Salt Lake City International Airport, with Utah Transit Authority buses, TRAX light rail and FrontRunner trains, at university campuses like the University of Utah and Utah State, at arenas such as the Delta Center, at ski resorts around Park City and Deer Valley, and at national parks including Zion and Arches. Local police departments and sheriff's offices, including Salt Lake City PD, Ogden PD and county sheriffs, are the ones who actually process turned in property under the state's lost property statute. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: What happens after I report a lost item to Utah police?
faq.a: Under Utah Code 77-11d-105, the agency that receives your found item has to publish and post notice of it. It cannot dispose of the property until at least eight days after that publication and posting, which gives you a window to come forward and claim it.

faq.q: How long do Utah police hold found property before releasing or disposing of it?
faq.a: At minimum eight days after the notice is published and posted, per state law. If nobody claims the item within nine days of publication, the agency notifies the person who found it, since finders can have a claim to unclaimed property. Some holders, like university surplus departments, keep items for thirty to sixty days before final disposition.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Departments typically ask you to describe the item and confirm one detail that was not made public, such as a serial number, a specific mark, or what is stored inside a bag, before releasing it.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Utah?
faq.a: No. Nothing in Utah's lost property statute requires a reward. Offering one is always your choice, not a legal obligation.

faq.q: Is it a crime to keep something you found in Utah?
faq.a: Yes. Utah Code 76-6-407 makes it theft to keep property you know was lost, mislaid, or delivered to you by mistake, if you do not make a reasonable effort to return it or turn it in to law enforcement.

intro: Vermont is one of the few states with its own dedicated lost property law on the books. Title 27, Chapter 11 of the Vermont Statutes actually spells out what a finder is supposed to do: give notice, in some cases advertise the find, and let the original owner reclaim the item before it can ever be sold or kept. That is a more detailed framework than most states offer, and it exists side by side with a separate unclaimed property system run by the State Treasurer for money, accounts, and similar assets that go unclaimed for years.

In practice, what happens to your phone, wallet, backpack, or laptop after it is lost in Burlington, Montpelier, or at a ski resort in Stowe still comes down to whoever finds it and whichever local police department or business ends up holding it. Officers, transit staff, and venue lost and found offices apply their own intake and holding practices on top of the state framework. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Lost property law, 27 V.S.A. Chapter 11
law.body: Vermont has a specific statute on lost property. It requires a person who finds lost property to give notice, generally to the owner if known or to local authorities, before treating the item as their own. A finder who fails to comply with the chapter can be held liable, and the original owner keeps the right to reclaim the property before any sale takes place.

law.title: Finder's duty to report
law.body: Under Chapter 11, a finder is not free to simply keep what they pick up. The statute puts an obligation on the finder to give notice of the find, which is why police departments across Vermont, from Burlington to smaller towns like Hartford, ask finders to turn items in or report them so the rightful owner has a real chance to reclaim them.

law.title: Unclaimed property, 27 V.S.A. Chapter 18
law.body: Separately from lost personal items, Vermont's Unclaimed Property Chapter covers money and intangible property such as bank accounts, uncashed checks, and refunds. Property is generally presumed abandoned after a dormancy period of a few years depending on the asset type, and it is then reported to the Vermont State Treasurer, who holds it in perpetuity until the owner or heirs come forward and verify their claim.

law.title: Local department holding policies
law.body: Individual police departments set their own practical timelines for physical lost and found items. For example, Hartford Police Department policy is to dispose of unclaimed property within thirty days unless other written arrangements are made, which shows how much day to day handling depends on the specific department holding your item rather than a single statewide clock.

law.title: Reclaiming and verifying a claim
law.body: Whether you are dealing with a police department under Chapter 11 or the State Treasurer's office under Chapter 18, the process to get property back involves proving it is yours. For unclaimed property claims through the Treasurer, Vermont requires the claimant to verify the claim, and local departments similarly expect you to describe or identify the item before releasing it.

VT.whereTitle: Where items end up in Vermont
VT.whereBody: Lost items in Vermont typically surface with local police departments in cities like Burlington, South Burlington, Montpelier, Rutland, and Hartford, or with the specific venue where they were left behind. That includes Burlington International Airport, Green Mountain Transit buses, Amtrak's Vermonter line, ski resorts and lodges around Stowe and Killington, and hotels, restaurants, and event venues across the state. Money and financial assets that go unclaimed for years instead flow to the Vermont State Treasurer's Unclaimed Property Division. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Does Vermont actually have a lost property law?
faq.a: Yes. Title 27, Chapter 11 of the Vermont Statutes is a dedicated lost property law. It requires finders to give notice of what they find and lets the original owner reclaim the property before it is sold, which is more specific than what many other states have on the books.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: You still need to prove ownership. Departments and venues typically ask you to describe the item, including at least one private detail such as a case scratch, saved photo, lock screen, or serial number, before they release it, even after it has been logged in as found property.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Vermont?
faq.a: No. Vermont's lost property statute does not require finders to be paid a reward. Any reward is always your choice as the owner, not a legal obligation, and many people offer one simply to encourage a faster return.

faq.q: How long will Vermont hold my lost item before it is disposed of or handed over?
faq.a: It depends on who is holding it. Local police departments set their own timelines, for example Hartford Police Department disposes of unclaimed property after thirty days absent other arrangements, while unclaimed money and similar assets are not treated as abandoned until a multi year dormancy period passes and are then sent to the State Treasurer, who holds them indefinitely for the owner.

faq.q: What is the difference between lost property and Vermont's unclaimed property program?
faq.a: Lost property under Chapter 11 covers physical items someone finds, like a phone or bag, and is generally handled by local police or the venue involved. Vermont's unclaimed property program under Chapter 18 is a separate system run by the State Treasurer for money and financial assets such as old bank accounts or uncashed checks that a business or institution has lost contact with you about.

intro: Virginia does not have one single law titled "lost property" the way some states do. Instead, what happens to something you lose in Virginia depends on who ends up holding it. A city or county police department follows one statute, Virginia State Police follows a separate exemption written just for them, a college or university follows a different rule again, and money or financial assets fall under the Virginia Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act, which is administered by the state treasury and is really built for old bank accounts and uncashed checks, not your phone or backpack. Layered under all of that is Virginia's common law of finders and its larceny statute, which decides whether keeping something you found was legal or a crime.
ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: No single statewide finders statute
law.body: Virginia has never passed one general law spelling out what a finder must do with lost personal property. Instead, separate Code sections cover separate holders, cities and counties, state police, and public colleges, each with its own hold periods and disposal rules. Common law fills the gaps, and courts generally still expect a finder to make reasonable efforts to locate the true owner before treating an item as their own.

law.title: Localities hold and eventually sell unclaimed property, Va. Code 15.2-1719
law.body: When a city or county police department ends up holding property that is never claimed, the locality can sell it. Once the sale happens, the clock is limited, no claim, suit, or proceeding to recover the funds or the property can be brought more than three years from the date of that sale, so waiting too long to check back with a department can close the door for good.

law.title: State Police follow their own rule, Va. Code 52-11.4
law.body: Property that ends up in the hands of the Virginia State Police is handled under a separate section that specifically exempts State Police from the general Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act. In practice this means the agency that recovered your item, a local department versus State Police, can matter for how and when it is disposed of if unclaimed.

law.title: Colleges and universities, Va. Code 23.1-104
law.body: If your item is found on a Virginia college or university campus, a different section applies. The institution must hold lost or abandoned property for at least 120 days before selling it, and if it is sold, the net proceeds must then be held for at least 90 more days so the rightful owner still has a window to come forward and claim the value.

law.title: Keeping a lost item can be larceny
law.body: Virginia criminal law does not treat finding something as a free pass to keep it. Petit larceny is a Class 1 misdemeanor, punishable by up to twelve months in jail and a fine of up to $2,500, and knowingly holding onto property you know belongs to someone else, or receiving goods you know were stolen under Va. Code 18.2-108, can expose a finder to prosecution rather than ownership.

VA.whereTitle: Where items end up in Virginia
VA.whereBody: Lost items in Virginia typically surface through local police non emergency lines and property and evidence units like Virginia Beach's, through Washington Dulles International, Reagan National, Richmond International, and Norfolk International airports, through transit systems including WMATA Metro and Metrobus in Northern Virginia, VRE commuter rail, and GRTC in Richmond, and through venue lost and found desks at stadiums, beaches, and amusement areas along the coast. Add in the university system, from UVA to Virginia Tech to William & Mary, each running its own 120 day hold under state law, and you have a genuinely fragmented landscape. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to prove it is yours. Most Virginia departments and campus offices ask for a description that matches details not visible in a photo, things like a serial number, a case scratch, or what is saved inside a bag or wallet, before releasing the item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Virginia?
faq.a: No. Virginia law does not require anyone who finds or returns your property to be paid a reward. Offering one is entirely your choice, and many people who found an item are simply glad to see it get back to its owner without any payment at all.

faq.q: Do I legally have to turn in something I find in Virginia?
faq.a: Virginia does not have one blanket statute forcing every finder to hand items to police, but courts have long expected finders to make a reasonable effort to locate the owner, and deliberately keeping something you know is not yours can amount to larceny under Virginia's criminal code.

faq.q: How long will a Virginia police department hold my lost item?
faq.a: It depends on the department and the value of the item, since Virginia sets rules by holder rather than by one statewide timeline. For property a locality ends up selling because it was never claimed, the law gives you up to three years after the sale date to bring a claim for the proceeds, so check with the specific department that recovered your item.

faq.q: What happens to something I lose on a Virginia college campus?
faq.a: Public colleges and universities in Virginia must hold lost or abandoned property for at least 120 days before selling it, and if it is sold, the proceeds must be kept for at least 90 more days, giving you a real window to reclaim either the item or its value through the school's own office.

intro: West Virginia does not have a single statute that spells out what a finder must do with a lost wallet, phone, or bag, the way some states do. Instead, what happens to your lost property here depends on a mix of common law finder duties, West Virginia's larceny statute, the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act found in Chapter 36, Article 8 of the state code, and the individual policies of the police department, airport, or venue that ends up holding the item.

In practice, most found items in West Virginia go to the nearest police department, transit office, or venue lost and found, where they sit locally for a period set by that department. Money and certain property that a business or agency cannot return can eventually be reported to the West Virginia State Treasurer's Office under the state's unclaimed property law. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: No single lost property statute, common law and the Unclaimed Property Act apply
law.body: West Virginia has not enacted a dedicated lost and found statute that tells a finder exactly how long to hold an item or when to turn it over. Instead, common law duties to make reasonable efforts to locate an owner apply, and the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, West Virginia Code Chapter 36, Article 8, governs what happens once property or money is reported as unclaimed to the state.

law.title: Police departments must report unclaimed property to the State Treasurer
law.body: State, county, and municipal law enforcement agencies in West Virginia are required by law to file an unclaimed property report with the West Virginia State Treasurer's Office when property they are holding, including recovered stolen or found items, goes unclaimed, rather than keeping it indefinitely at the department.

law.title: Dormancy periods before property is treated as abandoned
law.body: Under West Virginia Code Section 36-8-2, most property categories are presumed abandoned three years after the owner's right to demand it arises, and holders must file their annual report of property valued at fifty dollars or more before November 1 each year. Property from a safe deposit box cannot be turned over to the state until 120 days after that report is filed, which gives owners a window to reclaim items before they move further into the unclaimed property system.

law.title: No deadline to claim property once it reaches the Treasurer's Office
law.body: Once property is reported and held by the West Virginia State Treasurer's Office, there is no time limit for the original owner to file a claim, the office holds unclaimed property in a custodial capacity until the rightful owner or heir comes forward.

law.title: Keeping a found item can trigger West Virginia's larceny law
law.body: West Virginia Code Section 61-3-13 makes simple larceny of goods valued at $1,000 or more a felony, grand larceny. Someone who finds property, identifies the owner, and knowingly keeps it anyway can face exposure under this statute or its lesser degree for lower value items, which is one reason most departments and venues push found items into a formal lost and found process rather than letting a finder simply keep them.

WV.whereTitle: Where items end up in West Virginia
WV.whereBody: Lost items in West Virginia typically surface at the state's airports, including Yeager Airport in Charleston, Tri-State Airport in Huntington, and North Central West Virginia Airport near Clarksburg and Morgantown, or with transit systems like the Kanawha Valley Regional Transportation Authority in Charleston and Mountain Line Transit Authority in Morgantown. Sports and event venues such as the WVU Coliseum, Milan Puskar Stadium, and the Charleston Coliseum and Convention Center run their own lost and found desks, and items left at state parks, casinos, and hotels around the Greenbrier and other resort areas usually stay with on site security first. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you will need to prove it is yours. Departments and venues in West Virginia typically ask for a description plus one private detail, such as what is saved in a bag pocket or a lock screen wallpaper, before releasing an item to a claimant.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in West Virginia?
faq.a: No, West Virginia law does not require a reward for returning lost property. Offering one is always your choice, and many people recover their items with no reward involved at all.

faq.q: What happens if no one claims my lost item?
faq.a: Local departments and venues generally hold items for their own set period before disposing of them, while money or property that reaches a state agency or business as unclaimed property follows West Virginia Code Chapter 36, with most categories presumed abandoned after three years and then reported to the State Treasurer's Office.

faq.q: Does West Virginia have a specific lost property law like some other states?
faq.a: Not a dedicated one. West Virginia relies on common law finder principles, its larceny statute for cases of intentional retention, and the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act for money and property that ends up escheating to the state, rather than a single lost and found code section.

faq.q: What if I find something and just keep it instead of reporting it?
faq.a: That can expose you to liability under West Virginia's larceny statute, Section 61-3-13, which treats knowingly keeping property worth $1,000 or more from its rightful owner as grand larceny, a felony, with lower value cases handled as a lesser offense.

intro: Wisconsin's found property law traces back to territorial days and still runs on the same basic structure: Chapter 170 of the Wisconsin Statutes tells a finder what to do with lost goods, a local police department holds the item and waits for the owner to step forward, and a separate state system run by the Department of Revenue handles unclaimed money and financial property that was never physically "found" at all. Wisconsin also backs this up with a theft statute that applies to people who knowingly keep lost items instead of trying to return them.
ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Wisconsin's Found Property Law (Wis. Stat. ch. 170, §§170.07-170.12)
law.body: Wisconsin has a real statewide statute for found property, not just local policy. A finder of lost goods worth $100 or more is required to give written notice of the found item to local law enforcement, with limited exceptions carved out under sections 170.105 and 170.12.

law.title: The 90 day claim window
law.body: Local departments applying Chapter 170, including county sheriffs, hold found property for 90 days after notice is given. If the rightful owner appears within that window and proves their right to the item, it goes back to them. If nobody claims it in time, the finder can become entitled to it.

law.title: Police custody in practice
law.body: Once an item is turned in, it sits with the police department or sheriff's office that received the notice, not with the person who found it, until the 90 day period runs or an owner shows up with proof of ownership.

law.title: Theft of lost property (Wis. Stat. §943.20)
law.body: Knowingly keeping someone else's lost property instead of reporting it can be prosecuted as theft under Wisconsin's general theft statute. It is a Class A misdemeanor when the property is worth $2,500 or less, with higher classifications as the value climbs above $2,500 and $5,000.

law.title: Unclaimed financial property (Wis. Stat. ch. 177, DOR custody)
law.body: Money, stock and safe deposit box contents are handled differently than a found phone or bag. Wisconsin businesses must turn these over to the Department of Revenue after one to five years of inactivity, and the state then holds them indefinitely with no deadline for the owner to come forward and claim them.

WI.whereTitle: Where items end up in Wisconsin
WI.whereBody: Lost items in Wisconsin move through a mix of city police departments, county sheriffs, transit lost and found desks, and venue security offices. Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport and Dane County Regional Airport in Madison run their own lost and found processes, as do transit systems like the Milwaukee County Transit System and Madison Metro Transit. Sports and event venues such as Lambeau Field, American Family Field and Fiserv Forum also log found items separately from local police under Chapter 170. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, but you need to prove it is yours. Wisconsin's found property process under Chapter 170 requires the finder to notify police, and the department releases the item to whoever can establish their right to it, so be ready to describe a private detail, like a passcode, an inscription, or what's inside a bag, that only the true owner would know.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Wisconsin?
faq.a: No. Wisconsin law does not require owners to pay a reward to get their property back. Offering one is always your choice, not a legal obligation.

faq.q: How long do Wisconsin police hold found property before it's released or disposed of?
faq.a: Under Chapter 170, once a finder gives written notice of found goods worth $100 or more, the item is typically held for 90 days so the owner has a chance to come forward and claim it.

faq.q: What if the person who found my item never reports it?
faq.a: Wisconsin law expects finders of goods worth $100 or more to give written notice to police. Someone who knowingly keeps lost property without doing this can be charged under the state's theft statute, Wis. Stat. §943.20, which is why filing a report with the local department matters even if you don't know who has your item.

faq.q: My lost item might be tied to money or a financial account instead of a physical object. Where does that go?
faq.a: Wisconsin routes unclaimed money, stock and safe deposit box contents through the Department of Revenue rather than local police. These funds are held indefinitely once reported, so there is no deadline to search for and claim them.

intro: Wyoming does not have one statewide law that tells finders exactly what to do with a lost wallet, phone, or bag. Unlike the roughly twenty states that have enacted dedicated lost and found statutes, Wyoming leaves most of that ground to common law, its theft statute, and whatever policy the local police department or city has adopted. Knowingly keeping something you know belongs to someone else can still expose you to a theft charge under Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-402, but there is no single Title 34 section that spells out a turn-in duty or a statewide holding period for personal property found on the street or in a business.

What exists instead is a patchwork. Some cities, like Cody, have codified a holding period in their municipal code for lost or abandoned property that ends up in city possession. Other departments, like Casper Police, publish their own found property policy with their own minimum listing period before items go to auction or disposal. Wyoming's separate Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, run through the State Treasurer's office, mainly handles abandoned financial property such as uncashed checks and forgotten accounts, not the phone you left at a Jackson Hole restaurant or the backpack left behind at a Yellowstone trailhead. ReportLost works inside this framework: we file reports with the right local departments, alert the places you visited, and your report keeps searching for a match during your entire search period.

law.title: Theft statute covers knowingly keeping lost property (Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-402)
law.body: Wyoming's general theft statute makes it a crime to knowingly take, obtain, retain, or exercise control over property that belongs to someone else without authorization. Wyoming courts and prosecutors can apply this to a finder who knows an item is not theirs and decides to keep it rather than try to locate the owner or turn it in, even though there is no separate lost property statute spelling out the finder's duty step by step.

law.title: No dedicated statewide lost and found statute
law.body: Wyoming is among the states without its own lost and found law comparable to what some other states have enacted. There is no single section of Title 34 that requires a finder to report a found wallet or bag to police, publish a notice, or wait a fixed number of days before treating unclaimed lost property as their own. In practice this means common law principles, the theft statute, and local rules fill the gap.

law.title: Local police departments and city ordinances set their own rules
law.body: Because state law is silent, individual departments and cities decide how long they hold found property before disposing of it. Casper Police, for example, keep listed found items for a minimum period before releasing them for auction or disposal. Cody's municipal code separately provides that abandoned, lost, stolen, or unclaimed property in the city's possession for 90 days without a claim can be disposed of. Other Wyoming cities, including Cheyenne, Jackson, and Laramie, run their own property and evidence units with their own intake and hold procedures, so the exact timeline depends entirely on which department is holding your item.

law.title: Unclaimed property law is a separate track for financial property
law.body: Wyoming's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, administered by the State Treasurer's office, requires holders of abandoned financial property, such as uncashed checks, dormant accounts, or credit memos, to send due diligence notices for amounts of $50 or more and file an annual report by November 1. This statute governs money and intangible property held by businesses and institutions, not personal items like keys, luggage, or electronics lost in public and found by another person, so it runs on a completely different track from everyday lost and found cases.

WY.whereTitle: Where items end up in Wyoming
WY.whereBody: Wyoming's biggest lost and found flows run through its airports, including Jackson Hole Airport, Cheyenne Regional Airport, Casper-Natrona County International Airport, and Gillette-Campbell County Airport, along with the visitor centers and ranger stations at Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks, which see enormous numbers of items left on shuttles, trails, and in lodges each season. City police departments in Cheyenne, Casper, Jackson, and Laramie each run their own property and evidence units, and venues like the University of Wyoming, ski resorts such as Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, and casinos and hotels across the state keep their own found item logs. ReportLost routes your report to the right ones for your city, and the city pages below give you the exact local contacts.

faq.q: Do I get my item back if someone turned it in?
faq.a: Yes, if you can prove it is yours. Most Wyoming departments and venues ask for a description plus one private verification detail, such as a passcode, a specific photo stored on the device, or the serial number, before releasing an item to you.

faq.q: Is a reward mandatory in Wyoming?
faq.a: No. Wyoming has no statute requiring a reward for returned property. Offering one is always your choice, and many people recover items with no reward at all through the police department, airport, or venue that has it.

faq.q: How long will a Wyoming police department hold my found item before disposing of it?
faq.a: It depends on the department. Casper Police, for example, keep found items listed for a minimum period before releasing them for auction, and some cities like Cody codify a 90 day holding window for abandoned or unclaimed property in city custody. There is no single statewide deadline, so check with the specific department holding your item.

faq.q: Is it illegal to keep something I found in Wyoming?
faq.a: It can be. Wyoming does not have a specific lost property statute, but if you knowingly keep an item you know belongs to someone else and make no reasonable effort to find or return it to the owner, that can fall under the state's general theft statute, Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-402.

faq.q: Does Wyoming have one law that covers lost and found statewide?
faq.a: No. Wyoming has not enacted a dedicated lost and found statute like some other states. Instead, common law principles, the state theft statute, and individual police department or city ordinance policies fill that role, which is why procedures can differ from Cheyenne to Jackson to Casper.
